CONMEE (Thunder Bay) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 150) to amend the Navigable Waters Protection Act, chapter 115. He said: When the Bill for the incorporation of the Ontario and Michigan Power Company was before the House for its second reading a short time ago, the leader of the House expressed the view that it would not be within the jurisdiction of a provincial legislature to incorporate a company with the powers that company was asking for. The hon. leader of the opposition expressed the view that a provincial legislature might incorporate such a company, but might not be able to confer upon it the power to carry out the objects proposed, but

it might obtain that power by making application under chapter 115. I am not going to pretend to decide which of these opinions is correct; that is not necessary to the purpose I have in view. But so far as my information goes, so far as I can interpret the statute, and so far as I can learn from legal gentlemen with whom I have discussed the question, it is at least doubtful if a company incorporated otherwise than by the Parliament of Canada could obtain under chapter 115 power to construct works of any kind in navigable waters. Sub-section 'a' of section 2 of that Act defines the works that may be so ratified. (2) In this part, unless the contract otherwise requires:
' Work ' includes any bridge, boom, dam, aboiteau, wharf, dock, pier or other structure, and the approaches or other works necessary or appurtenant thereto.
In section 3 of this Act, we find these words:-
Except so much of this part as relates t* rebuilding or repairing any lawful work, nothing hereinafter in this part contained shall apply to any work or structure under the authority of any Act of the parliament of Canada or of the legislature of the late province of Canada or of the legislature of any province of Canada, passed before such province became a part thereof.
That language, it would appear, excludes from the operation of part 1, chaper 114 (a) ' any works authorized by the parliament of Canada.' I assume that that is not to be construed to mean that the parliament of Canada could not pass a special Act to authorize that work, but that is the language of the section as it stands whatever interpretation may be put upon it; (b) ' any work authorized by the legislature of the late province of Canada or any work authorized by the legislature of any province now forming part of Canada, passed before such province became a part thereof.' I would submit that this does not exclude the rebuilding or repairing of any existing works, I assume that such works could be rebuilt or repaired under chapter 115. That section is well knowm to hon. gentlemen, and therefore I shall not take up time reading it. But section 7 of the first part, which is the question under review here, provides:-
The local authority, company or person proposing to construct any work in navigable waters, for which no sufficient sanction otherwise existed, may deposit plans thereof and a description of the proposed site with the Minister of Public Works, and a duplicate of each in the office of the registrar of the district, county or province in which such work is proposed to be constructed, and may apply to the Governor in Council for approval thereof.
The subsection provides for advertisement so that there may be public notice given. I submit that this provision goes no further Mr. CONMEE.
than the works specifically mentioned in subsection (a) of section 2, chapter 115, under the provisions of that Act the works I have mentioned, namely, any bridge, dam, wharf, dock, pier or other construction or approaches thereto. Beyond those specific works mentioned, there is no power in the Act giving the Minister of Public Works or the Governor in Council power to authorize other wrorks such as a diversion of navigable waters. I may say that a question in point has arisen in connection with the works proposed to be built on the Rainy river at Fort Frances. The company there had obtained from the province of Ontario a charter under letters patent to carry out certain works of development upon the river, under an agreement which they had entered into with the government of the province. They came here to get their plans approved, but the department would not approve of them because they had not the requisite legal authority. Section 1 of the Act provides with regard to the rebuilding authority, that the w'ork shall be a lawful one, and what constitutes a lawful work is defined by the Act, chapter 115:-
Lawrful work means any work not contrary to the law in force at the place of the construction thereof at the time of such construction.
It was held that they had no lawful authority to go on with the w'ork, and therefore could not get their plans approved. That was one reason, I presume, which caused them to ask for the Bill from this parliament, which they obtained in 1395. The provisions of the Act provide that the company shall, before commencing their work, submit plans and apply for the approval of the Governor in Council.
Pending the passage of the Act, a dispute arose between the municipality of Fort Frances and this company, and the municipality filed a petition. It appears there was a dispute about an agreement-that is, there were, it appears there were, tw7o agreements entered into. The first one was dated 17th March, 1904, but it appears another agreement was made, as alleged by the municipality without their knowledge, and dated the 19th of October, 1905. The municipality took exception to the ratification of the plans, but an Act w'as obtained from this parliament, giving authority to the company to get its plans ratified. It got them ratified by an order in council, and I want to point out that an amendment to the statute is necessary, first, to determine what class of works are to be covered by such orders in council that may be passed under the Act, chapter 115.
I am not very much in favour of legislation by order in council. I do not think it is the best form of legislation, and I be-

lieve that the question involved in this measure is sufficiently important to require some governing statute which would better protect the public interest
I need not take up the time of the House explaining the position but there is a very grave injustice to Fort Frances. The agreement between the company and themselves is dated 17th February, 1904. The other agreement was sought to be legalized by the Act which the company asked for from this parliament and which was refused. The Act, as it is in our statutes, makes no reference to the alleged agreement of 19th February, 1905, at all. It was refused owing to a compromise. The solicitors on behalf of the town and the company agreed that an Act should be passed, without giving validity to the agreement in dispute, because the town was advised that they could set it aside by action in the courts. Strange to say that agreement has found its way into the order in council ratifying the plans. It is recited in full, and is made one of the bases for granting the request for the ratification of those plans.
I do not pretend to say -what legal effect that will have, but the Act in question-I had occasion to refer to it a few days ago- had been set aside, so far as it is in the power of the provincial legislature to do so. They passed another Act declaring that the company was not bound by the restrictions contained in the Dominion Act. When the Department of Justice came to deal with this provincial Act in the report as to whether it was an Act that should or should not be vetoed-I will not take the time of the House in reading the report because it is quite lengthy-the view of the minister was that the Act was very questionable, that it was beyond the authority of the provincial legislature to pass, but-unfortunately, in my opinion he did not recommend the disallowance of the Act and stated that the matter might be determined by the courts. Here was a community that, to my certain knowledge, has spent several thousands of dollars trying to defend what was a natural water-power, a great water-power in their town, for five years, first in the legislature, and then here, and, in the end, after employing the best counsel this country could afford and taking every step they could take as a small community to protect their interests, they are now relegated to the courts to find out what their rights are. I submit that there should be something better than that to determine these interests. There are several instances where the present method is not as workable as it should be. The department gave, as another reason.^ in this instance, why they could not ratify the plans of the company that they were asking for power outside the enumerated powers in the
Dominion Act, formerly Chapter 92, now 115, they were asking for the diversion of a navigable stream. The Department of Justice,
I believe, was consulted upon that point at that time-I am speaking of the application previous to the passing of the Act by this House in 1905-and the Department of Justice, according to my recollection, pointed out that that particular character of work was not covered by the Act, that there was no power to ratify the plans to that extent, unless they were empowered to do so by Act of parliament. So, we have this condition, that, under the Act as it stands to-day, if we take the view that has been expressed here, no provincial legislature could legislate in regard to the construction of any work of that character in or upon navigable waters, and it is equally true, if the practice to which I have referred be correct, that this government, under the existing law, cannot, or, at least, should not, in view of the express provisions of the statute, ratify plans in regard to works of the character of diversions to which I have referred. I am not going to say that plans of that character have not heretofore been ratified. I happen to know that works have been established at the town of Sault Ste. Marie without the ratification of plans, on the assumntion that the provincial legislature had jurisdiction and that ratification was not necessary. Somewhat later, in dealing with its securities, the company found that to give stability to them, they must have legal power to maintain their works, and they came to this government to get that power. But, if I am not mistaken, they have not got it. because the power did not exist under the statute to enable the department to ratify works already constructed. The language of the statute is ' works proposed to be constructed '-not works constructed. If I am cor-rectlv informed. I assume that the company, in ordeT to get itself out of the dilemma, will have to obtain an Act of parliament, if they have not already obtained it. The same condition exists in regard to the Kam-inistiquia river, near the cities of Port Arthur and Fort William. The works have gone on there without submitting plans to the Dominion authority. Dams have been, built and a navigable stream diverted. and there is no authority whatever. I could enlarge on that question and show that both life and property are at stake in these transactions. There is the case of the Current river near Port Arthur. A waterpower was developed there and storage dam3 built holding back large bodies of water. Unfortunately one of these dams gave way and the torrent of water carried away structure after structure in its course, including the tracks and bridges of the Canadian Pacific railwav in the city. And we know that the result of that was that there was great loss of property and the loss of several lives.

And these works are in their infancy in our country. The same great danger hangs over the community in the riding I have the honour to represent owing to the works at the city of Fort Frances. There should be proper inspection during construction of such works. Therefore, I submit this Bill with a view to meeting the difficulty. The Bill is in tentative form, and I hope that the government will realize the importance of the question and will bring in legislation to protect the public interest better than it is protected under the Act as it stands at this time. I might say, in that connection, that I notice there is a Bill on the Order Paper, introduced by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur). I do not know its scope, but I hope it is in the same direction as this. I am not sure that this Bill will reach a second reading, and that is why I have taken so much time in making my remarks upon it now. I may say, in closing, that it is not my intention to press this Bill-which is in tentative form, and can, no doubt, be made to cover the points of danger to which I have referred.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

AYLESWORTH (Minister of Justice) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 151) to amend the Exchequer Court Act. He said:	This Bill consists
pf one section, to provide that the Crown, at its option, in any action which has been tried in the Exchequer Court, may appeal not to the Supreme Court necessarily, but, if it prefers, to the highest Appellate Court of the province. There are sometimes cases in which, though a comparatively small amount of money may be involved, very important questions of law arise on which the Crown would wish to appeal from the decision of the judge of the Exchequer Court, but the expense of such an appeal to the successful suppliant, if the appeal is to be carried to the Supreme Court, is so heavy that one feels great reluctance in advising the Crown to exercise its right. It is thought that a measure of this character would prevent that difficulty at all events, and give a useful alternative right of appeal to the Crown, if the Crown should be advised, to exercise it. There is upon the Order Paper another Bill which stands for a second reading, to amend the same statute in regard to the position of the registrar of the court, and the two Bills might usefully be considered together.
Does the hon. gentleman say that the right of appeal is limited to the Crown side of the case, or does the suppliant have the same right?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is extending it to the Crown only.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

If found blameless, as charged, he will be re-instated and will be paid for time lost at his stated rate of salary.
As this was the first intimation that the Intercolonial Railway officers had received as to what the demands were, nothing more than a preliminary discussion could follow, and it was decided to allow Mr. Pottinger proper time to consider these demands, and to formulate a reply to them. Accordingly the committee adjourned, and met again on the following day, when Mr. Pottinger presented his reply.
It became evident at this stage that the case divided itself into two distinct parts.
1.	Relating to general questions of the relations between the railway and its clerks and of appointments and organization.
2.	As to wages or salaries of clerks.
In Mr. Pottinger's argument he stated definitely that the Intercolonial Railway could not increase the pay of the clerks, nor adopt a schedule of salaries, but upon other points the Intercolonial were disposed to be conciliatory
The reasons for the railway declining to agree to the increase of wages were fully set out by Mr. Pottinger, and were such that the committee felt that it would be desirable to take up the other matters in dispute, leaving the question of wages to be discussed with the deputy minister at a later date, and all parties assented to this procedure.
Accordingly, and after a full discussion, the following matters were agreed upon by all parties in the form as undei

' Your committee are of the opinion that it would make for greater harmony, and better efficiency, if a system of class of classification of clerks were '''itroduced. Not only would the above results accrue, but there would then be an available scheme for promotion, which at the present time seems to be lacking, and which omission breeds discontent owing to the uncertainty of upward progress for efficient clerks who have by length of service and attention to the duties of their office earned the right to consideration in this regard. Just what system of classification should be introduced must necessarily be evolved by the officials of the railway who are more intimately familiar with the details of the busi-

ness of the Intercolonial than your committee can possibly be. The men involved must necessarily accept the classification determined upon, subject, of course, to the right which they possess of bringing to the attention of their superiors in office any improvement in such classification, which to them may seem desirable in the best interests of the service.
Overtime.
Clerks duly called upon to work beyond the regular hours of their daily service should receive a pro rata allowance for such overtime. The same rule should apply to Sundays. .
Holidays.
The two weeks vacation with pay should continue as at present.
Relieving.
When a clerk is relieving a clerk of a senior position or class, the relieving clerk should, after two weeks, receive the rate of pay of the clerk whom he relieves.
Length of Day.
Your committee do not feel disposed at present to make any recommendation with respect to the number of hours that should constitute a day's work- the present day is practically one of eight and one-half hours.
Promotion.
Your committee are further strongly of the opinion that, outside of the rare cases that arise where an exceptionally able outsider is brought into the service to fill some particular position requiring special knowledge and training, the principle of promotion of those already in the service should obtain, having due regard, of course, to efficiency and the requirements of the service.
Discrimination.
The men ask for the following clause:
' Clerks will not be discriminated against for being members of the Railway Clerks* International Union, nor for serving on boards of adjustment representing clerks, and will be given leave of absence and be furnished with free transportation for such purposes. They will also receive the same privileges for the purpose of attending their meetings on any part of the line, when it is possible to do so without inconvenience to the railway.
Mr. Pottinger stated that that was now the practice on the Intercolonial Railway and that there was no objection to an employee belonging to a trade union. This being the case, your committee need deal no further with this particular point.	.
10. No clerk is to be suspended, or dismissed, without just cause. Any clerk charged with, suspended or discharged for an alleged fault, the same shall be fully specified m writing, giving full particulars two days prior to any investigation, and he will have a full and impartial hearing, and decision will be rendered by the railway's proper official within a reasonable time after the written request has been filed. If found blameless, as charged, he will be reinstated and will be paid for time lost at his stated rate of salary.
After reaching this conclusion the committee adjourned to meet at Ottawa.
On September 28 the committee met in the Railway Committee room of the House of Commons and there were present Messrs. Mon9g-han, Gibb and Mr. M. J. Butler, Deputy Minister of Railways and Canals.
Mr. Butler laid his views before the committee on the question of increase of salanes and these coincided with those expressed by Mx-. Pottinger at Halifax, and further explained the inability of the railway to increase their expenses, owing to the fact that working expenses of the railway were very largely in excess of revenue, and no funds were available for any increase of expenses.
The committee further considered the questions involved and now submit the following additional recommendations:-
The committee after its investigation, is of opinion that, in the matter of wages, the system that obtains of appointing from time to time new men at higher pay over the heads of men long in the service and probably more capable of doing the work, is injurious to the service and unjust to the men. The remedy for this lies in re-organization, and the abolition of the existing system of appointment influenced by political patronage, which from the point of efficient working we find ample evidence to condemn as applied to the Intercolonial Railway.
The present staff is greater than is uecei-sary, and this is another element which discourages individual increases. If the aggregate amount paid now in salaries were divided among a staff equal simply to the requirements of the service, the men remaining could be better paid than they are now.
The re-arrangement of salaries could then he made on the basis of the value of the position and the work done, having regard of course to what is paid for similar work elsewhere, and the local cost of living as compared with such comparative centres.
At the present time the wages paid to those now presenting claims before us are not, owing to above reasons, what a fail- consideration would justify. Under the re-organization hereby strongly recommended, it is more than probable that the adoption of increase of from 15 to 20 per cent would not mean an appreciable addition to the operating expenses of the Intercolonial Railway, and would produce a more equitable schedule -of compensation for the staff retained.	.
We summarize our further recommendations as follows:-	,	,,
1.	Re-organisation in order to adjust tne number of employees to the actual requirements of the service.
2.	An increase as above suggested to the reorganized staff.

House resumed adjourned debate on the proposed motion of Mr. Fielding that Mr Speaker do now leave the Chair for the House to go into Committee of the Whole to consider the Ways and Means for raising the Supply to be granted to His Majesty.

['Mr. Speaker, as the hour is getting pretty late I will promise not to keep you very much longer. Since the budget speech was delivered we have heard a great many different kinds of arguments, but it strikes me that what the farmer and the average business man want to know is what amount of taxes they are paying at the present time.', "By looking at the record we will find that in 1896 each man, woman and child in Canada was paying $5.48 in taxation while at the present time we find that we are paying $11 per head. While we find that the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) showed a surplus on the year's business we also find, by looking at the records, that we are $46,000,000 farther in debt. It struck me very forcibly how this would affect the province that I come from. By going into the figures I find that the province of Manitoba's share of this debt is something over $5,000,000. We have in that province about 9,000,000 acres of land under cultivation, and the debt of last year means a mortgage of $400 on every section of land under cultivation in the province of Manitoba. I would like to ask the Minister of Finance what the debt of this country will be at the end of four years. I had read a good deal about the Minister of Finance but I had never seen him until I came to this House. From what I had read and heard of the Minister of Finance I never knew of him as a joker until he delivered his budget speech. I am sure that the Minister of Finance must have been trying to get off a joke when he told the House that this government was a government that had held the land for the settler. I wonder if he forgets that almost the very first action of this government, after they came into power in 1896, was to try and give 375,000 acres of our western land to Mackenzie and Mann. Does he remember this government selling 250,000 acres of our homestead lands in the west for the paltry sum of $1 an acre? Every government that has ever held power in Canada, whether Reform or Conservative, has always held the homestead lands as a sacred trust of the people, but when this government came inlto power they sold even the homestead lands. They sold thousands and thousands of acres of our best coal lands to speculators and their friends. They gave leases of thousands and thousands of acres of our beat grazing lands for a paltry sum and in some cases people could get these leases for almost a song. Does the Minister of Finance forget this government selling hundreds of miles of fishing rights in the western country for $10 per year, or, does he forget the timber limit deals that were put through by this government or that they even went so far as to traffic in the Indian lands? They were not .satisfied with dealing in the white man's lands but we find that they took advantage of the Indians. The Indians are the same as orphans in this country; they are the wards of the people, we have charge of their resources and yet this government go to work and sell to their friends 39,000 acres of their land for $9,017. The purchasers, in a few weeks, in fact, before the Mr. W. H. SHARPE.
deed is made out to them, turn it over to speculators for $101,813, thereby cleaning up, out of the Indian lands, over $90,000. Mr. Speaker, we have heard a good deal during this session about a man they call Bill Miner. Bill Miner took his life in his own hands, you may say, when he went into the Rocky Mountains, held up the Canadian Pacific Railway express and stole a sum of money from it. I consider that Bill Miner is a prince beside these men who hide themselves behind the law and rob the orphans of the country. I do not intend occupying the time of the House very long, but there is a matter I wish to bring before the government and the House and that is in connection with an interview that the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Sifton) gave his newspaper in Winnipeg on the 10th February last. It is as follows:
Bluff and Bluster-Mr. Sifton's Comment on
Mr. Roblin's Defence of the Voters' Lists.
Hon. Clifford Sifton, who arrived in the city Monday from Ottawa, was interviewed yesterday in regard to Mr. Roblin's statement in the legislature regarding the provincial voters' lists. Mr. Roblin claimed that the lists were clean and satisfactory.
Mr. Sifton said that the statement of Mr. Roblin was untrue and that Mr. Roblin knew it to be untrue. The lists were flagrantly stuffed as every one knew perfectly well who had anything to do with the late election.
The assertion of the provincial premier, Mr. Sifton said, was a piece of impudent bluff and bluster.
When the last election was over the right hon. Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) asked the hon. member for Brandon the reason why the elections had gone against him in the province of Manitoba, and the hon. member for Brandon made practically the same reply to the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister repeated that same statement, or pretty nearly the same statement, on the 22nd January last in this House. I claim that if the statement made by the Prime Minister on the floor of this House on the 22nd January last is true, and if the the statement made by the hon. member foT Brandon in this interview with the Winnipeg ' Free Press ' is true, I, for one, have no right to a seat in this House. If those statements are false, as I claim they are absolutely false, then the hon. member for Brandon has no right to a seat in this House. I do not intend to discuss the merits and demerits of the Manitoba voters' lists at the present, time, more than to say that the electoral lists for the province of Manitoba are the fairest lists that are compiled in Canada to-day. The judges have complete charge of the lists in that province and there cannot be one name added or one name stricken off without the sanction of the judges. I was elected in the constituency of Lisgar, Manitoba, by 105 majority, and if this government will ap-

point a royal commission to inquire into the lists in that constituency, and if they can find 106 Conservatives improperly put on that list, or if they can find 106 Reformers improperly left off that list, I will resign my seat, provided, the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Sifton) will agree to resign his seat if his statements are not true, as I claim they are not true. I hope, Mr. Speaker, T make myself clear on this question. As the hour is very late I will resume my seat.

Mr. Speaker, when the House adjourned yesterday I had been attempting, in a few hurried sentences, to express the opinion that this country had been fortunate in having had for the last 12 years in charge of its finances a minister who, in spite of strong attacks upon him from interested sources, had engaged in strenuous endeavours, and in a large measure successfully, to keep the tariff of this country on a revenue basis. I notice that some hon. members on the opposition benches do not agree with me as to his success in that matter, but I think the hon. member for North Essex (Mr. Sutherland) demonstrated very successfully the other day that the tariff had really produced the revenue.
Has it stood the test?

The best test of the effectiveness of a tariff for producing revenue is that it produces the revenue.
I will try to show this by a reference to other countries. You have a protective

tariff undoubtedly in Germany, and you have a protective tariff in the United States with the result that in both those countries last year there were enormous deficits in the annual exchequer, and the United States are looking forward to a much larger deficit this present year; whereas, under what I still claim is a revenue tariff, you have had a series of surpluses under the able administration of the Minister of Finance.
Germany and the United States have been building Dreadnoughts.

I do not know exactly what Dreadnoughts have got to do with what I was saying at the present moment, but I can assure my hon. friend that if he builds plenty of Dreadnoughts he will not hear much of surpluses in his lifetime, nor in that of his children or of his childrens' children. I think the greater credit is due to the Finance Alinister because of what I willingly concede to be the peculiar geographical position of Canada, being in close proximity, as she is, to the great protectionist country to the south of us. But, I do not think that a careful study, upon full information, of the condition of the United States as a high protectionist country, would encourage the government, or any government of this country, to depart from a tariff for revenue purposes. It may not be out of place for me to say a few words about how high protection has worked in the United States. I find, in talking with my friends in eastern Canada especially, that there is what I may call, without offence, perhaps, a disposition to be dazzled by the apparent success of protection in the United States. If it be the main object of a country to build up trusts and millionaires, I admit that success. There is no doubt whatever that the-United States has been successful in building up trusts and millionaires, and that through the policy of protection, but, I do not think, on reflection, that is a matter which should recommend itself to the thoughtful men of this or any other country, because the building up of millionaires means inevitably the aggravation of that problem of the terrible disparity between great wealth on the one hand and great poverty on the other, which has harassed the minds of human-hearted men since the dawn of history. But, if we depart from the consideration of millionaires, I do not think there is much evidence forthcoming that protection has been a successful policy in the United States. What, after all, has the United States done? I wonder if hon. members of this House have ever thought what the population of the United States is per square mile, for example, as compared with that of Great Britain. The United States is keeping 21 people upon the square-mile. Great Britain puts 21 people upon every square mile and then makes provi-

sion for 537 more. Great Britain has 558 people to the square mile to the United States' 21 and I contend, Sir, that the economic miracle of the nineteenth century is not to be found in the resources of a continent being able to keep 21 people to the square mile under protection, but that it is to be found in two little pin points, comparatively speaking, sticking out of the ocean, the United Kingdom, keeping 558 people to the square mile in, what Mr. Asquith recently claimed, a degree of comfort to be found nowhere else in the civilized world. I have not had the privilege that my hon. friend from Brantford (Mr. Harris) has had recently of travelling over the various countries to which he referred, but all the evidence I can gather confirms me in the belief that he is correct' when he says that Canada has come through the recent period of trade depression better than any country in the world and certainly better than the United States. What is the condition of the United States at the present moment with regard to the depression and unemployment? I wonder if hon. members are aware that with these 21 people to the square mile, during the first eight months of last year more people left -the United States than came into it. It is true that the balance was redressed a little in the last four months and that at the end of the twelve months there was a paltry immigration into the United States of 6,000 people. Does that mean that protection is working out to be a great success in that country? For years a million people have been added by immigration to the population of the United States every year, but last year, with its 21 people to the square mile only compared with Britain's 558, the gate swung backward to such an extent that as many people left the shores of the United States as came to them. The chairman of Lloyd's Bank, speaking to the annnal meeting of the shareholders, at the beginning of this year-and he knows something about trade and financial questions-claimed before that meeting of shareholders that the conditions of unemployment in Great Britain have been largely aggravated by workmen returning from the United States where they could not get a living to the overcrowded centres of those little islands. I give the House that fact for what it is worth. I think the authority behind it is, at any rate, worthy of the serious consideration of this House if it is wishful to bring a serious mind to the consideration of this question.
Now,' I should like to give the House another fact that may help to enlighten us as to how far it may be wise for the Canadian Finance Minister to allow himself to be influenced by the supposed success of high protection in the United States. In 1860 the United States had two and a-half million tons of shipping and in that same year the United Kingdom had four and a-quarter
million tons. At that time the United States bid fair to be the great competitor of Great Britain unon the seas. This is a very important question for any nation that wishes to achieve commercial supremacy, because, Sir, if we pass our minds down through history, I think it can be claimed that no nation ever achieved real commercial supremacy which did not have the enormous command of the seas. Take, for instance, the Genoese, the Romans, the Phoenicians, the Spaniards, the French in the eighteenth century, and then, the wonderful shipping of Great Britain, which is a proof that this is a sound position. In 1860 an important experiment was adopted by the two greatest trade nations in the world for the consideration of the world upon tariff questions. The United States betook itself to the system of protection and Great Britain went the opposite way. At that time the shipping of the United States was two and a-half million tons and that of Great Britain four and a quarter million tons. To-day, after sixty years of that experiment, the shipping of the United States has shrunk to one and three-quarter millions of tons, whilst Great Britain's four and a-quarter millions of tons have gone up to eleven and a quarter millions of tons, far surpassing a shipping record of any country. I do not want^ to labour this question too far, but if this House were to permit me I should like to offer it a piece of evidence of how protection has acted in the United States of America and from an authority that would not be impugned in the United States itself. I suppose that most of us will admit that Mr. Bayard was one of the most brilliant men that the court of Washington ever sent to the court of London as an ambassador. Mr. Bayard, while fulfilling his duties in that high position, was asked to address the Philosophical Institution at Edinburgh, an honour that is only conferred upon men of the very highest distinction. In addressing the Philosophical Institution of Edinburgh, he referred to the United States in connection with the kind of argument that I am trying to bring before the House to-day, and said:
In my own country I have witnessed the insatiable growth of that form of state socialism styled ' protection,' which, I believe, has done more to foster class legislation and create inequality of fortune, to corrupt public life, to banish men of independent mind and character from the public councils, to lower the tone of national representation, blunt public conscience, create false standards in the public mind, to familiarize it with reliance on state-aid and guardianship in private affairs, divorce ethics from politics, and place politics upon the low level of a mercenary scramble than any other single cause.
I offer these words for the consideration of every member of this House as furnishing a strong argument why Canada should

not follow in her fiscal policy too closely in the wake of the United States. I claim for the government which I have the honour to support very great credit for their having introduced the principle of a voluntary preference to British goods coming into Canadian market. I would like to make clear what at any rate my attitude is upon this question. Personally I would deal with any part of the world where I could exchange upon fair and profitable lines the surplus products of my own country for the surplus products of that other country. Great credit is due to the government of Canada for introducing this preference policy because in it they realized the present needs of Canada. I ventured to fight my election upon the platform that the two great present needs of the west are: greater transportation facilities and better markets, and, Sir, the great needs of the west are the great needs of all Canada. We are going through a period of development. The policy of the government is a policy of developing the west, and the development of the west means the development of our whole Dominion. And, if as I contend, markets are the great need of the west then the government deserves enormous credit for having given this voluntary preference to British goods which has tended to enlarge and expand our opportunities for trade. I have been surprised to read that when the preference policy was first introduced it was met from the Conservative side of this House by the statement that we were giving the old country something for nothing. That was a surprising argument to come from a Conservative party in this or any other colony of the empire, because I recall the fact that throughout the whole history of the empire the Conservative parties of the various colonies have always claimed a monopoly of patriotism and imperialism, and they have generally-in the early days of the colonies especially-managed to get a monopoly of the patronage as well. But, that argument of the Conservative party with regard to the preference had of course the graver demerit of not being a sound one. I should not have thought that a party that occasionally has what I would call ebullitions of imperialistic sentiment, would cavil at giving the old country something for nothing, and would have denounced it as a thing which brought discredit upon the government of the day. But, did we give the old country something for nothing? Why, to my mind that preference policy was not only a splendid jfiece of sane imperialism but it was at the same time a splendid piece of business. It was based upon a sound understanding of the conditions, and the only conditions upon which trade between nations should be conducted. In what does international trade consist; what are the principles which underlay the giving of the British Mr. M. CLARK.
preference? As I understand them they are extremely simple and can he stated in a very few words. International trade is an interchange of commodities; it is^ that and. nothing more. Money has nothing whatever to do with it. If I were to offer you in a single figure proof of that statement I should remind you that in the year 1906 the total trade of Canada with the other nations of the world consisted of $550,000,000 worth of exchanges, and that out of that $550,000,000 worth of exchanges only $16,000,000 was composed of gold and bullion, $7,000,000 of which went one way and $9,000,000 the other. If that be the extent of our international trade, and if it be desirable to build up that trade, then it follows that, as the Minister of Finance epigramatically said the other day: Sound trade is a benefit to the buyer and to the seller both; and, the only way you can do an international trade is by an interchange of surpluses, and the only way you can get rid of your own surplus produce is by taking the surplus produce of other people. These were the principles which lay at the root of the British preference. Tt was an independent policy on the part of Canada and it was a proper policy as I consider. I am bound to say that in reference to another kind of preference which is being discussed upon the other side of the Atlantic, the attitude of leading statesmen in this country-of my hon. friend the leader of the opposition as well as the leading statesmen of the government benches-has been absolutely unassailable, in that just as we claim in Canada the right to manage our own affairs in fiscal matters, so, an absolute right of the same kind must be left to the mother country.
Now, did the policy of the British preference justify the faith of those who introduced it? Of course, the moment we gave a preference for British goods in our markets, the imports came in, and that is what created fear in the minds of those who talked of giving something for nothing. But the moment the imports came in, the exports went out to pay for these imports, and that had a beneficial effect upon the country because not only did every import take an export but every import brought an immigrant. And largely as a result of that freer trade we have had the enormous expansion which has been witnessed in the fortunes of Canada during the last few years. I take it that a very brief view of the entire policy of this government will show that the development of one tariff policy along these lines is absolutely vital to the development of not only western Canada but of the whole country. Our policy is a policy of development and it would be so whichever party were in power. One party builds the Canadian Pacific Railway and another party builds the Grand Trunk Pacific, and Canada marches on the road of progress.

But in that policy of develoment as carried out by this government we have included an immigration policy which has brought settlers to till our boundless lands, and coincident with that we have a transportation policy destined to convey the surplus products of our country to the markets of the world where there is a demand for them. But the only way in which they can be sold to other nations is by taking the only payment that can be got for them, that is, the surplus produce of other nations. These are the principles which lie at the root of all international trade, and the sooner we in Canada realize this the better.
I think I am justified in saying that there is a very clear distinction between the two parties on the question of tariffs. The hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster), in his speech the other day, may be taken, I think, to have fairly well voiced, in two hours and forty minutes, the sentiments of the opposition side; and, although he did not give a very extended protectionist argument, as did my hon. friend from St. Antoine division, Montreal, (Mr. Ames), nevertheless he did refer in terms of pride to what has been called the national policy.
Hear, hear.

I understand, from the. 'hear, hear,' of my hon. friend, that that policy is one that is looked back upon with pride by the Conservative party. Well, Sir, if it could be proved to have been a national policy, such is my opinion of the patriotism of Canadians, and such is my knowledge of my own patriotism, that I believe they and I would become unanimous in its support. But I must say, after a careful examination of the claims of a policy of protection to be called national, 1 fail to find that it established any claim whatsoever to that title.
May I ask the hon. gentleman if he can tell us what reduction of tariff has taken place under the present government?

I think I made an admission on that side which should satisfy my hon. friend that I am not making a party speech-that on the general tariff there was as much reduction under the Foster tariff as there has been under the Fielding tariff. But if I wanted to deal with my hon. friend in a party spirit, I could easily say that if lie and the bon. member for North Toronto were so proud of the national policy, why did they run away from it? I think that is a fair retort to the interruption.
What item of the present tariff would the hon. gentleman reduce?

Mr. Speaker, I should be quite willing to discuss any point
that I am acquainted with; but I have always understood that there is a great latitude in a budget discussion, and I aim sure that my hon, friend will agree that a new member of this House should have that latitude extended to him, at least as fairly and as freely as any other member.
I wish to understand my hon. friend's argument, and therefore I simply ask him what item of the present tariff he would reduce if he had his way?

I think there will be no difficulty, unless in the hearer, about understanding my argument before I am done. I think a truly national policy should be national in its outlook, and I want to put it_ fairly to my hon. friend and to the opposition. When hon. members of this House or their friends outside speak in favour of a policy of high protection and increased duties, is their outlook a national one? I have heard the pleas of my hon friend from Peel (Mr. Blain) and others for an increase in the duties on woollens. Would it be argued that anybody who was pleading for an increase in the duties on woollens was doing so out of the warmth of his consideration and affection for those who wear woollens. There are 5,000 people all told employed in the woollen trade of Canada, and there are seven million of people using woollens. I should say that people who have a national outlook in their policy would look to the seven millions rather than to the 5,000. When the hon. member for Brantford in the last parliament (Mr. Cockshutt) advocated in this House holding the duties on agricultural implements as high or higher than they were when the present government reduced them by 21 per cent, does anybody believe that the hon. gentleman and his friends were actuated by a sincere desire to get cheap agricultural implements for the hundreds of thousands of farmers who are coming into our western country? I do not want to be uncharitable, but I think the outlook of those gentlemen was sectional. And if I dare say a word about the province of Nova Scotia, I should even direct a question into that quarter. My hon. friend from North Toronto was very severe on the Finance Minister in connection with certain proceedings in Nova Scotia. I am not sure that there is not some little symptom of protection down in that part of the world; but I should be very lenient in my judgment of it, because I have stated very sincerely the grounds on which I think this country ought to be grateful that it has bad such a Finance Minister as the member for Queens and Shelburne. And I should be lenient to him in Tegard to what happened in Nova Scotia, on another ground because I should always wish to recollect that that country is inhabited by a race of men who are reputed to keep the

Sabbath and everything else they can lay their hands on. And I think the lines of the great Scottish poet apply in such a case :
Then at the balance let's he mute,
We never can adjust it;
What's done we partly may compute,
But know not what's resisted.
But even in the case of any protectionists that there are in Nova Scotia, I fear it will be found to be true, if we examine it carefully, that their outlook is narrow, sectional and provincial rather than national. I fail to see how protection ever works in any other way, and I fail to see that its outlook ever entitles it to the high-sounding name of national policy. _ Show me where it is a national policy in its operation as between the various classes of a country. It is constantly happening in the high protectionist countries of the world, that goods are sold in enormous .quantities more cheaply abroad than they are in the country in which they are produced. A well informed American, intimately acquainted with the iron trade, told me the other day that in Pittsburg, in the month of January, 1908, steel rails were sold to the American people in pursuance of a national policy at $28 a ton, and on the same date were sold in Middles-borough on the north-east coast of England for $19.50 a ton. Now, if it be a national policy to rob your own people in order to sell cheaply to foreigners, with the incidental advantage of building up a few millionaires in your country, then a policy of high protection is a national policy, but otherwise it is not. Not only in its outlook but in its operation and its effects the National Policy in Canada proved to be no national policy because it failed to build a nation. When I was pursuing my campaign last year, I invested a modest sum in the purchase of the Canadian Almanac, and I found the trade figures of this country, which were there given, most instructive. It gave the figures beginning in 1883 and concluding in 1906, and these figures showed that the total trade of Canada, in the year 1883, after the National Policy had got fairly under way, was $230,000,000. I passed my eye down the column until I came to 1895, and I found that in that year, after 12 years' experience of nation building under the National policy, our total trade had actually fallen to $224,000,000.
What about the home market?

I was not living in Canada at that time, but I have a friend in western Canada, who is now doing splendidly in the little town where I live, and who was a Conservative until he voted for me, and he told me that in those

days he carried a letter six weeks because he could not buy a stamp to put on it.
I was pursuing the same line of argument . in the town of Red Deer during my contest and I was met with the same interruption about the home market. I replied that the home market in those days was pretty well illustrated by the fact that if a farmer went out with his gun and was lucky enough to shoot a rabbit he got his dinner, but otherwise he had to go fasting. He retorted there are no rabbits just now. I said: That's sure evidence that the Laurier government is going back to power because otherwise Divine Providence would have to provide the rabbits.
My hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) passed on to another portion of his protectionist argument, on which he touched very gingerly, and that was the balance of trade. On that point he contended himself with quoting the figures and showing that the balance was against Canada. I cannot say that I was surprised at that line of argument, because I have read other budget speeches by the same hon. gentleman and have heard him use a similar argument at much greater length. But I am bound to say that this theory of the balance of trade is an extraordinary theory to one who has studied economics in the school founded by Adam Smith. The balance of trade is against Canada, argued the hon. gentleman, because our imports exceed our exports. Just let the House consider for a moment. How is that balance of imports over exports brought about? We are spending enormous sums on an immigration policy to produce it. If the theory of Adam Smith be the correct one, there is no such thing in the actual operation of trade as a balance. An import always takes an export in the actual interchange of trade. When there is an excess of imports over exports or the reverse, there is also a method of accounting for it, apart from the actual exchange of trade. In the case of Great Britain, her enormous excess of imports over exports is accounted for by goods coming to pay the interest on her enormous capital invested abroad and the cost of the shipping she does for nearly every nation in the world. But it is a common question to ask: What about the enormous excess of exports by the United States over the imports? But does it not occur to any one who reflects that Great Britain has an enormous amount of capital invested in the United States which must be paid for by American exports, and the payment of the interest on that capital debt accounts for the excess of exports from the United States to Great Britain.
Tell us about the unemployed in Great Britain.

stone said, ' No Chancellor of the Exchequer is worth his salt who shrinks from economy in detail.' I have seen nothing but what is admirable, nothing but what the younger members of this House may admire in the way my hon. friend leads the opposition in moderate criticism of expenditures in detail and fair examination of the estimates in this House. I endorse his attitude and action in that matter. But I remember very well also Mr. Gladstone saying another thing, and that was that your expenditures depend upon your policy. In regard to that matter, our policy being a policy of development, I take it that it is impossible to avoid great expenditures and great growths in expenditure in this country. But always it should be provided, I think, that these growths in expenditure are wise growths. And certainly Mr. Gladstone set his face, not only to economy in detail but to economy in wise policy, and especialy in regard to the very dangerous expenditures upon armaments. Now, my hon. friend (Mr. Foster), as he has been reminded in this debate, went down to Prince Edward Island last year, and made a proposition which,^ I think, was not a very necessary proposition for the development of this country. And I would submit to him that, after all, he cannot pose as an economist with a proposition to build a twenty-five-million-dollar tunnel in one hand and a proposition to build a fleet in the other.
How about the Newmarket canal?

The Newmarket canal, or any ditch, might be of use, if we have a sudden invasion of Germans for building defences behind. I should like to say a serious word to this House and to the government upon military expenditure in general. But I do not think that a singleword of my own is needed if the House will allow me to read a quotation from some memorable words of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) spoken outside of this House:
Surely, while our obligations toward the empire are very great and binding

And to that I fully subscribe.
yet our first and paramount duty is to the people of the Dominion whose servants we are.
And now, I think, when I have referred to the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) as a, pessimist, I shall have finished anything I wish to say about him at this time. I have tried to deal with him as a protectionist, a prophet and economist. He also posed in his usual role as a pessimist in this country. Now, it is always safe, whatever subject the) hon. gentleman may be dealing with, to assume that, if

there be a gloomy side of it, he will find it. I was surprised, early in the session to find him consumed with dread lest Canada should run out of fish. I think that was the most extraordinary fear that ever oppressed a human mind. A little later in the session, his fears had been removed from fish and concentrated upon the Germans. And now, he has a dread of Canadian credit sinking in the money markets of the world. I must say that I do not share with my hon. friend his spirit of pessimism in regard to the budget statements of the Minister of Finance in regard to the future of Canada. My hon. friend made what I cannot think a very successful attempt at alliteration in describing the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) with two P's. If I might endeavour to better it, I would describe the hon. member (Mr. Foster) as a Pessimistic Promulgator of Panics. I cannot help thinking that I can give an explanation of how he takes so kindly to that role. Early in the session he did me the honour to reply to a few remarks which I had taken the liberty of addressing to the House. And in this reply he compared himself to an ox. Well, it is a perfectly possible thing for an hon. member of 'this House to have exaggerated ideas of his-,own proportions. But if that be the description that he cares to go under, I do not know, Sir, that I have any right to quarrel with it. He reminds me of that very useful and domestic animal, the bull, that can be thrown into a state of purposeless and groundless panic by the simple exhibition of a red rag. My hon. friend goes about with a red rag stretched in front of him. If what he said about the falling credit of Canada had come from any other member than Die member for North Toronto, I am sure it would have received from the people of Canada more .attention than it will now receive, and more attention than I feel inclined to give it. The credit of Canada, to my mind, is as sound as her prairies are boundless, and the spirit of her people is indomitable. Talk to me about the credit of Canada! I came out as a professional man, with some school boys, seven years ago, and I am tilling to-day a thousand acres of land, and am able to make at that occupation far more than is necessary for my family and myself. There is a picture of the heritage that we are working out, and it is a picture which begets, in my mind at any rate, and in the minds of the great majority of Canadians I am sure, not a spirit of pessimism but a spirit of optimism. I was glad to notice the other day	that

These three features are: First, the increased amount which year after year the government has drawn in taxes from the pockets of the people; secondly, the lavish expenditure of those sums; and thirdly, the so-called surplus. The first and second of these features have already been dealt with at some length by hon. members on this side of the House; ! will detain the House but a short time in referring to the third outstanding feature, that of the so-called surplus; in other words, the surplus upon consolidated revenue account, or to be strictly accurate, a balance upon a part only of the financial transactions of the year. I think it will be admitted by hon. members on both sides of the House that the two principal objects sought to be attained in keeping the public accounts of Canada are first, to present to the taxpayers a clear and true statement of the management of their finances by the government, and to show honestly the result of the year's transactions; and secondly, to keep a permanent record of those transactions.

Why, Sir, a continuation of such surpluses would strain the credit of the country, notwithstanding the fallacious financial reasoning of my hon. friend from Red Deer. Now, there is a system followed by the present administration of charging to capital account items of expenditure which properly should be charged to consolidated revenue account. One instance of this is to be found in the bounties which formerly the Conservative government charged to consolidated revenue account but which the present Finance Minister charges to capital. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) has admitted that had he last year charged the total bounties of $2,250,000 in round numbers as he said, to consolidated revenue account (as the Conservative government had done) instead of to capital account, his estimated surplus of one and a half million dollars for the year just closed would not only have disappeared but be would have had to acknowledge a shortage on consolidated revenue account alone of $750,000-the shortage on the full year's business be it remembered was over $46,000,000 to the 31st of March, 1909. Let me point out very briefly wherein the evil of this system lies. It tends to show fictitious surpluses upon consolidated revenue accounts where in reality deficits exist or may exist, upon that account if all these items are charged against it as properly they should be. The government of the day, any government, can have but two objects in view in the practice of such a course; first, to create fictitious surpluses upon consolidated revenue account with which to dazzle the eyes of the taxpayers and, second, to prevent by such means the true and actual condition of the treasury being appreciated by the country at large. Any such surplus is only a bookkeeping expedient; the real surplus, the surplus the country wants to know about and is entitled to know about is the surplus available to be applied in liquidation of the public debt. It is contended by some that the severing of accounts and the showing of surpluses on a part of the year's transactions, namely consolidated revenue account, makes no real difference, because the outcome in the end is the same. But, Sir, the showing of a surplus on one account and a shortage or a deficit on another is quite as objectionable as that of presenting two budgets one showing a surplus and the other a deficit. C.
