And, in support of this view he quotes 'Stourm', an eminent authority on public finance. I submit that the result to the country of the practice of the present government in this respect, is inconsistent with the country's best interest. There are two evils attendant upon the figuring out of these immense balances-for they are not really surpluses-on a part of the year's transactions. In the first place they are an invitation to extravagance; an invitation which the government has been unable to resist. In the second place they tend to lessen watchfulness of the administration by the Canadian tax-payer. The prevailing system of declaring these so-called surpluses has furthermore reached a stage where it is not unattended with considerable danger to the country. In the first place it misleads a too confiding public and diverts attention from the fact that the public debt is rapidly increasing; and in the second place it encourages the government to pursue a course of extravagance . and to assume on behalf of the country unwarrantable financial obligations. Still further, the result of these glowing and growing surpluses dangled before the eyes of the man who cannot or does not examine the public accounts for himself, is, that his senses are dulled to the fact that the country is getting year after year deeper and deeper into debt. So it is, that when any proposed expenditure is advocated, that portion of the public which is misled is prone to say: 'Well, we had a surplus of two millions, or five millions, or nineteen millions of dollars last year and we can very well afford it;' whereas, if their attention were directed rather to the increasing debt than to the vanishing surpluses they would be more inclined to say: ' We increased our public debt by two millions of dollars, or five millions of dollars, or forty-eight millions of dollars (as it was last years) and we must proceed carefully.' Let me say here, Sir, lest I should be misunderstood in that regard, that I fully recognize the fact that in a country such as Canada where we are laying the foundations for the future prosperity of our people (foundations which must be broad, and deep, and enduring), the government is from time to time justified in making expenditures beyond revenue, and against the credit of the country. But granting this, would it not have been better for the government to have been perfectly frank and straightforward with the country by charging to consolidated revenue account everything which should be charged against it, and by directing attention to real shortages Mr. JAMESON.
upon the entire business of the year rather than to incorrectly computed surpluses upon a part only of the year's transactions? For I say without fear of successful don-tradiction, that notwithstanding any explanation or excuse which may be made to the country on the part of the government, this grave fact remains to confront the people of this country, that not only have these immense surpluses, aggregating, as the Finance Minister has told this House, $114,500,000 absolutely disappeared, but a vast shortage has developed. To meet this shortage, the government presided over by the right hon the Prime Minister, has mortgaged every home and every acre of the Canadian tax-payers in the amazing sum of $65,500,000, and that without a proper knowledge thereof being held by the country at large. Now, this brings us to the point where we may reasonably ask, would it or would it not be well for the government of the right hon. the Prime Minister, as well as the government which is to succeed it, and all future governments of Canada, to be perfectly frank, perfectly honest and perfectly straightforward with the country in regard to matters of finance.
Hon. gentlemen opposite have said, during the course of this debate, that we on this side of the House criticise, but do not offer suggestions. I propose, with the consent of the House, to make a suggestion in regard to the statement of the public accounts. There might, it seems to me, be profitably added to the public accounts a statement showing: first, interest-bearing assets of Canada; secondly, non-interestbearing assets of Canada. I am aware that a committee is now engaged in revising these Dominion assets after a long term of years; but I think it would be advisable to revise them once every four or five years in order that the dead wood might be cut out. That would tend also to keep a closer watch on arrearages and prevent them from becoming seriously stale, and perhaps entailing a loss on the country. There might also be stated, all new obligations of the Dominion incurred during the year, including guarantees whereby the country is made secondarily liable. The present system of dissevered public accounts, which has been in vogue in Canada since confederation, has the greatest claims on our respect, because it was adopted by the fathers of confederation as in their opinion best suited to the needs of the new Dominion. Forty years ago confederation was an experiment. Many people were sceptical of the result; many were openly hostile to the new order of things. The revenues of the country were less than one-fifth what they are to-day. The business of the country was comparatively insignificant; the population was small; the railway mileage was light; the country was unopened, comparatively un-

known, and little thought of. The credit of the new Dominion, which would be requiring to borrow large sums of money abroad for its development, was naturally a matter of the utmost concern. It is not strange, then, that the system of severing the public accounts, dividing them into capital account and consolidated revenue account, was adopted in order that the revenue of the new confederation might be placed alongside of the ordinary expenditure, to show that the country justified its new dignity. But, Sir, forty years have passed, and confederation is no longer an experiment. It has proved itself and justified the faith of its founders. The country has develoned, its population and industries have increased; it is well and favourably known abroad, and its credit, until recently at least, has been excellent. But the early form of the public accounts does not seem to have shared in the general progress. They lack a clear and direct 'statement of account, showing in brief the result of the year's transactions, what may be termed the 'cash turnover.' The statement of receipts and disbursements on pages 12 to 17 of the public accounts is very much involved. A great deal of it is made up of cross entries, so that the total of $426,000,000 is no indication of the amount actually disbursed on account of services of the Dominion. In this statement are included savings bank and trust funds, which are not receipts and disbursements on acount of the securities of Canada. Here is an item of over $26,000,000, Bank of Montreal, London, on the side of receipts, and the corresponding item is $34,000,000 on the side of disbursements. Here is an item of $164,000,000 "cash credits" on the side of receipts, and the corresponding item is over $160,000,000 on the side of disbursements. These are cross entries, which largely affect the totals. They are necessary in an account kept as this is, but they confuse rather than tend to simplify the account, which is unintelligible to the man in the street. This account fails to show in plain figures the amount of cash in the treasury at the beginning of the year and the amount in the treasury at the close of the year.' It is necessary to turn to the balance sheet at page 4 of the Public Accounts involving totals of over $481,000,000, to find this. Now, I repeat what I have before stated, that I do not mean to say that the adept cannot take the public accounts and by examination of them find how the finances of the country stand ; but to the average citizen of Canada they do not convey any adequate idea of the actual condition of the country's finances from year to year. There should be, I believe, a complete statement which would do this, and which could reach the people throughout the country, through the medium of the press. Neither the present involved statement nor the budget speech of the Minister of Finance accomplishes this. Would it not be well therefore that the public accounts should contain an additional statement showing the cash turnover, a statement showing the total receipts on the one hand and the total disbursements on the other, and indicating the balance for the year, whether it be in favour of or against the country ? The report of the Secretary o'! the Treasury of the United States contains a statement somewhat along this line, indicating the result of the year's transactions, and yet of such moderate length that every journal in the^ country can well spare the space to publish it in full for the information of the public at large. Again, the financial accounts of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland for the fiscal year begin with a direct statement of the amount of cash on hand at the beginning of the fiscal year- so much in the Bank of England and so much in the Bank of Ireland-stating the receipts under different heads on the one hand, and the expenditures on the other, and ending 'balance in the Bank of England,' 'balance in the Bank of Ireland.' I am aware that the system of public accounting in Canada is not the same as that employed in the United States or in Great Britain; but I contend that their systems are much more simple than ours, and ours should be made as plain as figures can be made to read. Such a statement, it seems to me, could not be open to any objection, and would be productive of good results. It might fittinglv be placed at the very outset of the public accounts, to show the actual receipts and expenditures, with the totals of each-in other words, the cash turnover. Such an account, when it showed a surplus, would show a surplus which would be available for liquidation of the public debt, and, when it showed a deficit or shortage, would clearly indicate the added debt of the country. It may be said that by shelving a large deficit or shortage in the public accounts of Canada in years when there were large expenditures on capital account, as has been the case during the year just closed, when the total expenditures showed a shortage of $46,000,000, the credit of the country might be prejudiced.
But let me say that whilst the severed accounts may mislead the man in the street, they do not deceive the men who lend the money. The money-lenders have a due and proper appreciation of the real state of affairs. Furthermore, to say that a frank and open statement would injure the credit of this country is obviously to imply that our credit now rests on deception, and that is a view I cannot entertain and hardly think any hon. member would entertain for a moment. But the Canadian tax-payer is after all the man who should

know the best and the worst. The public accounting is largely for his information. It is his business that the government is conducting and it is to him the government must account. He is entitled, to use a western expression, to a fair show-down once a year, and the duty of the government is to give him a fair, honest and frank statement. Then when the public debt was increased, the government must show justification for that increase by the exigencies of the occasion or by public works of a permanent or reproductive character and the Canadian tax-payer would be in a position to pass judgment on its wisdom.
Now Sir, I do not propose to address the House at greater length upon this subject. I will only add that as the Canadian taxpayer is yearly entitled to a clear, straightforward statement of the finances of the country, no government which fails to give it does all its duty to the people, who in the end must be called upon to pay the bills.

My hon. friend from Digby (Mr. Jameson), who has just given to the House a very clear and concise criticism of the methods of bookkeeping in this country, took some umbrage, at the beginning of his address, at a passing, jocular reference by my good friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) to our good friends from Nova Scotia, and of course took up this pleasantry in a very serious vein. And I noticed that when lie did so, our good friends opposite applauded him. Now, Mr. Speaker, I have one way of defining the different classes of people in different countries. I have no disposition to favour the Scotchmen or the Englishmen or the Welshmen or the foreigner or, the French Canadian. If I were to take umbrage at everything I hear about Englishmen, I would have a great many complaints to make, for I hear derogatory remarks concerning them every day. What I have to say about national descrimina-tion of that description is this, that you have good and bad Scotchmen and Englishmen, and people of every kind. Wherever you go, you will find some good and some bad, and my good friend, the member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) was simply making a jocular reference to our good friends in Nova Scotia, which my serious friend from Digby took in so serious a manner.
My hon. friend made some complaints about the increasing expenditure of this country and its consequent increasing taxation. I agree with him that there are two principles which every government ought to respect. One is to keep down as low as possible, consistent with the reasonable expansion of the country, the taxation of the great mass of the people; and the second and the most important necessity

is to keep down the cost of the commodities which have to be consumed by the great masses of the people. But I submit that by no system can the expenditure in a new and growing country be prevented from increasing. Nations are like individuals. The young man, who has no one but himself to keep, and who has a salary of $1,000 a year, will live within his income if he is prudent. But if he gets married and has a family and increases his salary to $2,000 a year, imperceptibly he spends that $2,000 a year. This is a great country in process of development; and I submit that while there is every reason and need for economy, it is impossible for this new and growing country to develop, as it ought to develop, without increasing its expenditure. Look over the list and you will find our expenditures increasing right along; and although there is a temporary arrangement to curtail them this year, we may depend upon it that the channels of trade and the development of our country will always necessitate an increasing outlay. There are false notions and ideas about economy. Economy is not parsimony. It does not consist in refusing -to pay what is legitimate. True substantial economy is well spent money, and I have some slight criticisms to make as to the method which my good friends the government themselves may adopt with regard to this system of retrenchment.
My hon. friend from North Toronto made a slight reference to what he called the enormous increase in taxation. My hon. friend from St. Antoine Division (Mr. Ames) made a protest against what he called the system of mortgaging the interests of future generations. With regard to increasing taxation, he calculated the amount at $11.50 per individual. I want to say this: In looking over the United States revenue, taking the sum total of their custom and excise revenues and dividing that by the population, I discovered that their tax per head was equal to $6.50.
My hon. friend from North Toronto takes the revenues created by the customs and excise in Canada for the year 1908. divides that by what I think a reasonable estimate of population, 6,500,000, and finds a per capita tax, or individual tax, of $11.50. In that connection, I wish to consider the principle contended for by my hon. friend from St. Antoine, that we ought to pay our debts as we go along, that we have no right to transfer anything to the future. On the contrary, I contend that under no economic principle operated by any government is it possible to entail upon future generations financial disadvantages that at all compare w'ith the mighty advantages that the present taxpayers are providing for future generations. The fundamental basis

of my hon. friend's complaint was a fallacy; the difficulty is exactly the opposite of what he states, the difficulty is how to develop a young, large and growing country without imposing extraordinary taxation upon a small present population. The principle is seen in the very figures I have given,- with a population of 88,000,000 and an income of $500,000,000, you find a per capita tax in the United States of $6.50; but, take the tax revenues of this country and divide them by a population of 6,500,000, and you have a per capita tax of $11.50. The principle demonstrates itself. Will anybody say that there is nothing in these mighty productive national expenditures for future generations ? Are we building transcontinental railways for to-morrow? Are we deepening the canals of this country for use next week? Are we broadening and deepening the channels of trade in this country for a few weeks or months to come? Are we determining the fiscal and commercial policy of this country to meet the wants of only 6,000,000 people? No, the expenditures which make, this taxation necessary are largely to provide machinery for the development of this country thirty years from this time. The obligations that wo are placing upon future generations are far more than counterbalanced by the assets we are creating for the future. And these assets develop and increase in importance, and any liabilities that may be placed u; on the people of this country thirty years from now will be far more than paid by the increasing values of the assets that are beiAg created by the expenditures of to-day.
You cannot prevent the future taking the responsibilities and meeting the obligations created by the present unless you establish the economic principle that we should do things just for to-day. The sound national policy is to look ahead for a hundred years, and, when we are bearing the burden of a financial obligation created by the construction of a great transcontinental railway in the year 1909, we may calculate that the real benefit of that expenditure will be felt the more effectively a hundred years from now. If, then, the benefits are for the future, why should not the generation that is coming pay for these things? In this connection I have a protest to make against what I regard as an unwise stipulation of this government with regard to certain public expenditures. I have laid down the principle that we must have expenditures in this country, that we must have increasing expenditures. I have stated what I think about the principle of economy-that economy is not always in withholding. And on that point I would refer my hon. friend to what is said in the good old Book itself, 'There is that seattereth, and yet increaseth; and there is that withholdeth more than is meet, but it tendeth to poverty.' I take this opportunity to protest against withholding necessary expenditures when that withholding will decrease the returning revenues. So far as the country I represent is concerned, I believe that necessary expenditures. are being withheld, the withholding of which will decrease the revenues to the Dominion exchequer from that part of the country. If I can prove that position then I say the policy is a very unsound one.

But that does not interfere with the nature of my complaint. I say it is important at the present time that Canadian fish should be protected against poachers

from the United States. What the government ought to do is to make the people on the other side realize that we are going to protect our own interests. Now, the provision that is made in the estimates this session, I am afraid, is not likely to accomplish that object. These are what I call revenue producing principles, these are what I call productive expenditures, and every productive expenditure ought to be provided for. I recognize that the government should make some retrenchment. I do not say that they should be economical, for that would imply that they had been wasteful. But I do say that, owing to conditions that have arisen, largely from the conditions in the United States, it is necessary for the government at the present time to exercise retrenchment and care.
I think after all that the government is to be complimented upon even the present financial condition in this country. Sir, two weeks ago I had the privilege, with one of the influential business men of Pittsburg, to go down into the coal mines in the vicinity of that city. I spent over a week looking into industrial conditions of the United States, going down into the mines and studying everything belonging to the industrial conditions of that country, and it is after a man has gone through an experience of that kind that he is prepared to regard even the worst conditions in Canada as favourable in comparison. I want to say that the coal miners of England 50 years ago were in a better condition than the coal miners in the surroundings of Pittsburg are to-day. Factories are closed, or only producing 50 per cent of their usual output. To show how thankful we ought to be that we have not been more affected by the commercial conditions in the United States, let me point out that wherever you have in Canada productions depending upon the American market, there you have depression. For instance, in the city of Nanaimo and its surroundings, about 50 per cent of the coal production has to find a market in the United States, and that industry is depressed for the reason that in California and other western states many factories have been closed, and there exists a general stagnation in manufacturing enterprises which affects the market in British Columbia. I repeat that after my experience in one of the chief industrial centres of the United States, our industrial classes in this country have reason to be thankful that they are so well off in comparison. Nowhere in Canada, that I am awaTe of, is there anything to parallel the condition of the workers in the steel rolling mills of Pittsburg, and in the coal mines of that district. Why, in hours of labour, in wages, in the price of the commodities that they require to use-and that is the true test of the condition of workingmen-out in-Mr. RALPH SMITH.
dustrial classes in Canada are very much better off than those in that old settled community of Pittsburg. Why, Sir, it costs more to live there than it does in the city of Ottawa, a community hundreds of years younger. The purchasing power of the wages earned by the Pittsburg workingmen is a good deal less than the purchasing power of the wages earned by our Canadian workingmen. Everything depends on that principle. It is not the money that the wage-earners gets and puts into his pockets at the end of the month that tells the tale, it is what that money can purchase of the commodities that he has to buy. It is in the amount of the necessaries or comforts of life that the wage earner can purchase for his wages that you can calculate his true relative condition. I do not hesitate to say that the purchasing power of the wages of thousands of men in the United States, where so many factories are closed down, where so many others are working at half time, where there are so many thousands of idle men-the purchasing power, I say, of the wages of workingmen in the district I visited, is in no way to be compared to the purchasing power of the wages of men in this country. Therefore I say thht we have reason to congratulate ourselves that we are so favourably situated, although we are in an exceptional bad state in the coal mining regions of the Pacific coast.
Now I wish to ask whether the government are making a proper selection of the objects upon which to expend the taxes of our people. I will be frank with pay hon. friends in the government in saying what I am about to say. I admit that retrenchment is necessary, but I am going to say that you cannot make the people believe that retrenchment tin productive works is necessary in face of the fact that you spend $7,000,000 on the militia of this country.
I do believe that if there was a band of men, I might say a political party, that went through this country from one end to the other, preaching the policy of a reasonable curtailment of military expenditure, they would obtain the votes of the majority of Canadians. I say that when you cut down expenditures on productive public works and devote them to militia purposes, you are saving at the tap and wasting at the bunghole. When you expend $7,000,000 in the present financial stringency and interfere to that extent with the productive works of this country, you are making a great mistake. I say there is no justification for spending $7,000,000 on the frills and fripperies of militarism. I am speaking frankly to the House. I will tell you what I would do with the $7,000,000 that is now expended on the militia.
I do not know what it is for. I can quite understand the necessity of defence if you know that there is an existing

enemy, but I am not aware of any. Where ia the possible approaching enemy of Canada? Where does he live? Do you say in the United States? There never was a time in the history of this country when the feeling between this country and the United States was as friendly as it is at the present time. Where is the enemy to come from? What are you spending the money for? Is it fashionable to have a militia? I know it is proper to have a reasonable measure of protection and have it better distributed in Esquimalt as well as Halifax and other points. My hon. friend from the city of Vancouver (Mr. Cowan), very seriously, in a speech that he made the other day in Vancouver, urged the government of this country to make adequate provision for assisting in the protection of the empire, but * I want to tell him that if the citizens of Vancouver had the right to make a selection between the deepening of the harbour of Vancouver and supporting the militia they would support the former principle. If my hon. friend has to report to the people of Vancouver that he cannot secure an expenditure for the productive works of that city, which are necessary for the development of its trade, they will ask him why it was that he supported the principle of such an enormous expenditure on military matters when he did not get the money necessary for the productive operations of that community. I am not a military man, but I am not a man of prejudice. I have my own personal ideas but I always try to look on both sides of every question. This is something that the people of Canada do not want to this extent at present. They are an innocent, self-reliant, enterprising people, attending to their own business every day, cultivating their farms, developing their mines, enlarging their factories, looking after their" domestic interests and improving this great country not only by developing its natural resources and increasing its wealth but by developing the finest manhood to be found in any country in the world. That, Sir, is the greatest contribution we can make to the empire. By establishing in this country an ever _ increasing population, true to the British institutions that we possess, by developing the great resources that we have and by surrounding the people by moral influences and inculcating amongst them high principles we make the best possible contribution to the empire. If you are going to provide for further contributions to the British navy take three and a half or four million dollars of the present provision for militarism in this country; take half of what you provide for militarism if you are going to make the necessary contribution to the British navy, but, there can be
no support of and there can be no agreement to the curtailment of the necessary expenditures upon works such as I have mentioned that are revenue-producing, that are creating and developing this country and -that are building up its trade. To my mind by so doing you are losing at the tap and saving at the spigot. The people of Canada, under the present conditions, at a time when you have to restrict your expenditures, are not likely to support a principle of that kind. With no enemy in view they are not prepared to support a principle of that kind if the productive interests of this country have to suffer in consequence.

Mr. Speaker, before six o'clock I was dealing with the necessity of the government maintaining as far as possible its ordinary expenditure on productive public works, and I said that while there was considerable evidence that certain important public works in this country were not provided for in this year's estimates, we nevertheless have provided for an expenditure of $7,000,000 on the militia. Now, Sir, I do not repudiate the position that it is necessary to have a reasonable provision foT a military force in Canada; I believe that our coasts should be protected by fishery cruisers and that there should be efficient police supervision and protection along the boundary line. But what I did say and what I repeat is, that a time when you have to restrict the ordinary expenditures of this country in its present state of progress and development, is not the time to expend $7,000,000 of the people's money for military purposes and that whatever is spent ought to be better distributed to the advantage of the Pacific coast.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I want to bring to the attention of the House a question that has not been considered by us so far, but it is nevertheless a question which deserves the serious consideration of the government and of the members of this parliament. I refer to the question of free importation of bituminous coal into Canada, by agreement of reciprocity with the United States, which has become a live issue of late on account of the action taken in regard to it by the Congress of the United States. Hon. gentleman will have observed that the United States Congress at its special session, has provided in the schedule of tariffs for the possibility of reciprocity in coal; and let me ask the Minister of Customs and the Finance Minister especially to give their attention to this. The question as I

have said has not been presented before in this parliament, possibly because there was no opportunity such as that which the policy of the United States Congress has recently afforded, t shall endeavour to show that there is no one policy that could be adopted by Canada that will contribute so much to our development, especially to the_ development of the western country, as reciprocity in coal between the United States and ourselves. I know that our friends in the far east, as coal producers, may take reasonable objection to the facts as I shall put them, and I have every respect for their opinion in that regard. I have every consideration for the large and permanent and successful investment in coal operations in Nova Scotia, but it must be remembered that we have coal mines in British Columbia and in Alberta as well, and I want to point out that the geographical situation of this country makes the offer of free coal from the United States one of the greatest boons that has been placed at our disposal for many years. When provision was made in the tariff of the United States for a possible reciprocity in coal, a strong public feeling arose in British Columbia on the question. I probably represent more of the coal mining interests of that province than any other member from British Columbia, and I have been appealed to not only by the consumers of coal, but by the British Columbia coal operators themselves to . bring this matter to the attention of the government. I shall present evidence of this feeling in British Columbia, and if the United States Congress should continue to make the necessary provision for reciprocity in coal, then I shall make the modest request of the Canadian government that they a'ive careful consideration to this important matter and take advantage of any offer that they may make.

As indicating the public sentiment on this subject, let me quote the following article from the daily press of the Pacific
coast:
Anything that affects an industry in a community is of interest to the residents in that community and it naturally follows that the interest taken corresponds to the importance of the subject under discussion. Just at this time the United States congress, both the Senate and House of Representatives con-''eued in special session, are in the midst of a tariff discussion. The tariff being of vast importance to all classes, it is not strange that the Bill introduced by Congressman Payne, as chairman of the Ways and Mean* Committee and bearing his name, comes in for so much discussion, both for and against, and which discussions are of world wide interest.
It is, however, generally believed that the Bill will be passed and become law substantially as reported by the Ways and Means
Committee. To Canadians the question naturally arises, how will the Dominion be affected by the provisions of the Payne Tariff Bill. Among others the Bill calls for reciprocity timber and coal under certain conditions. Many other articles in which Canada is interested are also affected, but the ones of paramount interest to the whole of Canada are lumber and coal. Eliminating for the present the lumber question from the discussioji, for while lumber is of great importance 'to British Columbia and to Vancouver island, coal holds a most prominent position in any discussion bearing on Vancouver island resources. In the Payne Bill it is proposed to put bituminous coal on the free list with any country granting similar conditions. Under the- Dingley, or present tariff, sixty-seven cents per ton duty is paid on every ton of coal shipped from Nanaimo, Ladysmith or Union to San Francisco, Puget Sound ports and Alaska. There is no foreign coal shipped into British Columbia. Quite a lot of American coal, however, finds its way into the prairie country through the lake ports; Port Arthur on the upper end of Lake Superior being the principal point of distribution to the prairie country. Nova Scotia ships quite a little coal into the New England States of America, and under reciprocity a larger market for Nova Scotia coals will be found in that territory. Again, by reciprocity Canadians who reside in the prairie country and long distances from Canadian coal mines would he supplied at reduced rates from across the line; and similarly the coal mines (f Canada could and would reach farther into the States for trade.
Meantime what does Canada gain or lose with reciprocity in the exporting and importing of coal? With the exception of Nova Scotia mines, which theoretically might lose a little Canadian territory, the rest of Canada would he greatly benefitted, and we of British Columbia and Vancouver island would gain immensely in the territory that could be covered by Eastern British Columbia mines and also the Island mines. It is reported that during the past year the Western Fuel Company shipped some 70,000 tons of coal to Seattle, Tacoma, Bellingham and other Sound cities, to say nothing of the San Francisco and San Diego markets. They have shipped coal even as far as Spokane in the State of Washington; and if given reciprocity can very largely increase the territory to be sup-idied, sufficiently so to keep the Island mines all running at full blast for years to come.
Vancouver Island mines, however have one rival for the coast markets, and that is Australia. The Australian continent can, and does, produce cheap coal; and although it is not in the same class with the Vancouver Island product, it can be mined and sold cheaper. We of Nanaimo have a vivid remembrance of the effect on our prosperity v hen the San Francisco coal yards were filled with Australian coal. Officials of the Western Fuel Company state that they have not the slightest fear of Australian coal in competition outside of San Francisco, and not to any extent there, unless some advantage be given that coal.

Lindsay, president and superintendent of the Crow's Nest Coal Company for many years, and Mr. D. D. Mann, an owner of coal mining interests in Nova Scotia-I read the following references to this question in view of the 'changes made in the 'tariff of the United States. Mr. Lindsay stated:
In bituminous coal and coke, if Canada reciprocates, there is an enlarged and increased American market for British Columbia. As Canada imposes no duty on coke, the American duty will be removed. Canada does levy 53 cents on bituminous coal, so reciprocity is a condition here.
Mr. Mann made this statement:
Mr. Mann stated that there should be no duty on coal.
The geographical positions of the two countries show that, he said. * Here in Eastern Canada, in Ontario and Quebec, we have no coal, while to the south of us is an unlimited supply. In the western states there is no coal, while to the north, in Canada, is another 1 Mr. RALPH SMITH.
unlimited supply. Why should not there be free trade in coal? If there were it would do away with the long haulage over the railways from coast to coast in Canada, and from coast to coast in the States.
Now, Sir, I want to bring to the attention of parliament the investments in coal mining in British Columbia and Alberta. The operations in coal in Nova Scotia have depended almost entirely, until recent years, on a foreign market in the United States. My hon. friend from Cape Breton, who spoke the other day in support of a resolution in favour of higher duties on coal made the statement that it was important that a protective duty should be placed on coal in this country to preserve the Canadian market for coal products. The difficulty in British Columbia is to get markets for our coal products, and the very natural conditions of the country determine that for all time to come, a large part of the coal products of British Columbia will be dependent on foreign markets. I want to say, in passing, for the policy of the government, that ten years ago, previous to the disaster in San Francisco, 90 per cent of the coal produced in British Columbia went into the American market. There never would have been coal mines in British Columbia but for the American market. The Hudson Bay company, in operating the coal mines of British Columbia 50 years ago, found their whole market in the United States. I am happy to say that at the present time 60 per cent of the product of these coal mines is consumed in Canada and 40 per cent in the United States. I mention this to show that there has been more real development of a home market for the coal mining industry in British Columbia in the last 10 years than there was before that since confederation. This fact is very important, that whereas 10 years ago only 10 per cent of the coal produced in Vancouver island was consumed in Canada, to-day 60 per cent is consumed in Canada. But since the financial panic in the United States the mines have been working only two-thirds of the time, owing to the contraction of the United States market, from the closing of their factories and the shrinkage in business resulting from their financial condition. Let me give to the House the present condition of coal operations of British Columbia and AlbeTta. We have in British Columbia the Wellington Colliery company, the Western Fuel company, the Crow's Nest Pass Coal and Coke company, the South Wellington mines, the Vancouver-Nanaimo Coal Mining company, the Nicola Valley Coal and Coke company, since McGowan & Co. of Vancouver, and since 1907 the Canadian Pacific Railway company has begun its mines at Hosmer. We have in British Columbia a total capital invested in coal mining operations of $20,000,000, employing 7,000 miners directly

and maintaining a population of 30,000 people. The yearly product-1907 is the latest year I have been able to get-is nearly 2,000,000 tons, and its approximate value is $7,637,713. The total known coal areas in British Columbia, which I have collected from the Geological Reports of Canada, are 1,123 square miles, containing 38,642,000,000 tons of bituminous, 20,000,000 tons of anthracite, and 314,000,000 tons of lignite. These axe known areas. Of course, there are large coal areas in British Columbia of which very little is known. The total export of coal from British Columbia to the United States in 1907 was 733,224 tons, amounting, as I have said, to 40 per cent of the total production; so that if we had reciprocity in coal, British Columbia would practically monopolize the markets in the western states of America.
In this connection I want to mention that I have made some inquiries with reference to the coal production of Alberta, and the same is largely true there. There are about eighty companies producing coal in Alberta. This is principally bituminous and lignite, with a little anthracite. These companies are capitalized at $40,000,000, and have a total capital invested of about $15,000,000. I was surprised to find the large amount of wages paid and the large amount of the output of these mines.
The money paid in wages in the province of Alberta in that production is equal to $3,500,000 per year and the number of hands employed averages 37,800. The total yearly production in 1907, including coke and briquettes, is equal to 1,958,112 tons. The total coal area, according to the geological reports, is as follows: "19,589 square miles, containing 44,530,000 tons of bituminous, 400,000,000 of anthracite and 60,000,000 of lignite. So that the House will see that, in the development of these enormous coal areas in our great west, a free market in the United States would be a
great advantage. The development of these coal areas depends very materially upon the United States markets, so that, if there be no disadvantage unduly to the rest of Canada and if it be in the interest of Canada generally, this government should take advantage of any offers, if any be made by the United States, to giv our coal a freer entry into their markets. Let me draw attention to another fact. The central provinces of Canada are non-coal producers. Take for instance Manitoba. There may be some coal of an inferior quality in that province, but I do not suppose that for many years to come it will be able to produce sufficient coal to supply its own needs. At present it depends on imports from the United States for about 98 per cent of its coal consumption. In Ontario there is no coal, and the probability _ is there never will be any. Ontario is a great manufacturing, largely populated province, depending absolutely at present-as it will, in my opinion, have to depend for all time to come-on the imported article. I do not think it is possible by any improvement of transportation facilities, and taking into account reasonable competition, to have a sufficient investment of capital into the Nova Scotia mines as will enable them to supply the market in Ontario. I have in my hand a very important statement which I have compiled from 1899 to 1908 showing the quantity of foreign coal imported" into Canada during that period, and what I ask the House to remark is the constantly increasing imports of that commodity. A few days ago the Minister of Finance received a document from the representatives of the gas industry in Canada. I do not know its value, for I have not looked into this question. But I received, as other members have, a copy of this document, and I want to read a few paragraphs:

That is not correct.

-Gas companies within recent years have been compelled to stop using, notably Montreal and Quebec, who formerly used Nova Scotia coal. (2) Because transportation charges from Canadian coal fields were prohibitive.

If the hon. gentleman will permit me:	Is he aware
that the great grievance of these people is that this government permits coke to be brought into this country free of duty, and that what they want is a duty on coke?

I think that, further on in the document, they do ask that. But I think that the statements in the two paragraphs I have read call for explanation on the part of those who oppose this principle. Now, I wish to say a word further with regard to the Nova Scotia position, for which I have great consideration. I have here a document, I do not know the man who wrote it-Mr. W. C. Milner-
Oh, oh.
I do not know who he is.
We do.
Perhaps he is a Tory.

Certainly,-a good
one.

Mr. Milner read a paper before the Mining Society of Nova Scotia, in which he presents facts and figures to show that Nova Scotia coal could find a market in New England if there were no duty, and that at the same time the home markets would be safe. I cannot read the whole article, but I wish to read a few paragraphs. As I have said, it is a public document, read before an important institution in Nova Scotia, by a citizen of that province, and it speaks for itself. How much it is worth I cannot say. I read it to the House, and it will be to my hon. friends from Nova Scotia to disprove the statements this gentleman makes:
The importance of United States trade, not only to the maritime provinces but to all Canada, was such that in 1849 all the governments of Canada united in a joint effort to extend it. . . In coal, the United States became early our chief market.
I want to point this out in passing. What I am contending for in the great west is that, logically and naturally, the permanency and extent of the coal mining operations must depend upon the foreign markets, which, according to this document was absolutely true of Nova Scotia fifty year ago-they depended upon the New England markets for the development of their mines.
In coal, the United States became early our chief market. It was not until after 1820, that the production of the Nova Scotia mines exceeded 10,000 tons per annum; in 1826 it exceeded 100,000 tons, and in 1850, 200,000 tons, and of this output the United States purchased considerable more than one-half. In 1853, when the duty was 24 per cent ad valorem, the shipments were 120,000 tons out of 217,000 tons of an optput. The shipments rose from 120,000 tons to 404,000 tons in 1866, the year reciprocity was abrogated. Of the entire output of our mines-558,000 tons- United States purchased over 400,000 tons, or about four-fifths.
There are other items in this document that I have marked, but I do not consider it necessary to read them. But I felt it my duty, as a member from the Pacific coast province, to bring this matter to the attention of the House. The last thing I have to say on the question is this: That, with regard to certain products, coal included, it seems to have been the policy of the federal government of Canada, since the first days of confederation, to hold out an opportunity to the United States to provide for reciprocity in certain articles. As this document says, in 1879 the great national policy itself provided for reciprocity between the two countries on certain natural products, especially on coal and Mr. RALPH SMITH.
coke. In referring to the tariff schedule of 1906, I found provision was made for holding out an opportunity to the United States to meet Canada in certain reciprocal changes; power was given the Governor in Council to take advantage of any tariff reductions in the United States. But in this new tariff of 1907 the government did not continue that long standing offer to the United States. Now I want to make an appeal to the Minister of Finance to consider this question. I notice that provision for reciprocity has not been inserted in the new proposed tariff sent up to the Senate of the United States. When I was in the United States two weeks ago I made special inquiries with regard to this matter, and I was told that there would almost certainly be a reduction in this particular coal down to 40 cents a ton. If the same provision were in the tariff schedule of Canada that existed in 1906, then he would have the power to take advantage of that reduction in the duty which we have not to-day. I want to present that consideration to the government, so that if the United States provides for reciprocity in coal, we may be able to meet them. Speaking with all consideration for Nova Scotia, I do not see why she ought not to be able to compete in the Canadian markets as well as in the markets of New England. There is nothing I know of which can conduce so much to the development of the great west as the possibility of getting better markets in the United States for the bituminous coal of Canada.
Now I want to make an appeal to my hon. friends from British Columbia. I have no doubt the Minister of Inland Revenue will use all his influence with the government in reference to this matter. I think my hon. friends from British Columbia are interested in the development of that province as much as I am, and here is an opportunity of doing something that will help to develop the great resources of that province. Anything that will lessen the pressure of protection in this country I will be glad to support, and anything that will extend protection I will be loath to support. I know that most of my good friends from that province are supporting a party that stands for adequate protection, which means a general advance in the tariff of at least 20 to 25 per cent, and I can understand how difficult it is for them to support me in this principle. But I hope, because of their loyalty to the province, that [DOT]they will lend me their influence to accomplish this object. I am sorry to say however, that I am not so sure of the support of my hon. friend from Vancouver (Mr. Cowan). Of course he has expressed his great zeal for the development of British Columbia. As a matter of fact, I have been

using my good influences to keep his feet in the straight and narrow path ever since he came down to this House, and I perceive that he still needs that influence. I ,was sorry to read a speech he made the other day in Vancouver. While I think I may appeal with some confidence to my hon. friend from Kootenay (Mr. Goodeve), and to my hon. friends from the other constituencies, I have not the same confidence that my hon. friend from Vancouver can use his influence in favour of my proposition. I say that because of the wild and extravagant statements he is reported to have made some days ago to his constituents in Vancouver. It seems to be the misfortune of my hysterical friend from Vancouver that whenever he finds his feet he looses his head. I feel a great sympathy for him in my heart, but I think I have discovered that he is afflicted with political spasms. Now political spasms, like physical spasms, are always an evidence of weakness. I want to read my hon. friend a report of the speech he made at Vancouver in order to give him an opportunity of taking back some of his statements if he can do so. If he cannot take back those statements, then in my opinion I think he has lost his public influence in this country in so far as it can tend to the advancement of the interests of British Columbia. I say with every feeling of kindness to my hon. friend, that when a public man stands up in the great commercial city of Vancouver, as he did, and utters the slander that he did against the leader of the Liberal government of this country, he is bound to loose his influence for good. The strongest weapon that any representative in this House is entitled to use is the weapon of argument, the weapon of reason, but when he makes the statement he is reported to have made in reference to ministers of this government, charged with great responsibilities, I think he has seriously injured the public influence that he ought to seek to retain. He discussed that question of better terms with British Columbia, also the old chestnut of Oriental immigration. I thought my hon. friends would never dare to open their mouths again about Oriental immigration. I notice that my hon. friend from Yale-Cariboo (Mr. Burrell), speaking in Toronto, told the people how important it was that the yellow race should be kept out of Canada, but he did not tell them that he himself employs men of the yellow race. The rest of my hon. friends from British Columbia are in the same position. In discussing the question of better terms my hon. friend from Vancouver spoke in this .manner of the attitude of the Prime Minister on that question:
Then Sir Wilfrid had turned to the question of better terms and in rather sneering tones had cited the Conservative proposal to 1504
refer that question to an independent and impartial tribunal. . . . They had no difficulty in showing Sir Wilfrid and the House of Commons that the Asiatic problem had been projected into the public life of Canada by the blundering treaty making of the government.
Hear, hear.

I hope my hon. friend will just keep up that response for the next sentence.
It did not trouble him to show that every province in Canada was entitled to a fair and impartial hearing of its claims.
Now here is the sentence to which I wish to call his special attention:
It was a white livered coward who would deny British Columbia an independent, fair and impartial, tribunal for the settlement of her claims .
I say, with the greatest regard, that, if my hon. friend said so, and he will have an opportunity of disproving it, any public man in this great country who stands up on any platform and places himself on record by making such wild and prejudiced statements, disqualifies himself from occupying any important place or exercising any influence in the public affairs of the country. He went on further to say:
He had had an opportunity of saying to Sir Wilfrid that it was left for him to be just and be a man. . . But he would say now that he had not the courage of manhood to treat honestly and fairly with British Columbia and submit to an impartial tribunal a claim, the justice of which was admitted by the highest courts in the land. From this time forth it would be his bounden duty to tell the public that in his judgment, whatever it was worth, that man was a false alarm in the public life of Canada.
_ I consider it fair to my hon. friend, cherishing as I do, nothing but the kindliest considerations towards him and, as a political missionary, being out for the Vancouver sinner-as long as the light holds out to burn the vilest sinner may return-to give him an opportunity of explaining these statements. If my hon. friend is prepared to take the responsibility of these statements, I say that he has done the greatest possible injury to himself. If, on the other hand, he is prepared to take the responsibility of saying that he did not make these statements, that he had been falsely reported, it is due to himself to let the people of this country know it.

Yes, Mr. Speaker, as has been said, I wish merely to reply to the references which have been made to myself. In doing so I am prepared to credit the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Smith) with the best motives, at least the best motives that could actuate that hon. gentleman. I take it that he has given mei this opportunity of explaining the report of the speech I made at Vancouver. I have not read that report. I would be glad if he would let me see it. I assume that the hon. gentleman realizes, as we all do, that when reporters seek to condense the remarks of a speaker, they very often omit the arguments and use such catch phrases as will make good reading. I want to thank the hon. gentleman for giving me this opportunity of explaining the remarks I made at that meeting in Vanvouver, but I want to remark, before proceeding to that personal explanation, that the position which the hon. member for Nanaimo finds himself in in this House seems to me somewhat bizarre. From his place amongst the faithful on the other side of the House he has charged the government with dereliction in the matter of the fisheries of British Columbia, he has charged the government with militarism

Mr. COWAN -and he has charged the government with a neglect of its duty in the matter of coal. The position of that hon. member is rather a peculiar and anomalous one. I will not say that it is apropos of that position although I want to remind the House that on the American side of the line in their political terminology they have one expressive word-mugwump. A mugwump, they define to be something on the fence with his mug on one side and his wump on the other. I want to say in justice to the government, with reference to some of these criticisms and in loyalty to the truth, that it has been dealing recently with the protection of the halibut fisheries on the Pacific coast, and I will say here, as I said on the public platform in Vancouver, that I believe the government is honest and sincere in its intentions. As I understand the intentions of the government, they are that it will improve the fishery protection service on the Pacific coast. The government knows, I believe, quite as well as the hon. member for Nanaimo knows, that in the last year there were
49,000,000 pounds of halibut poached by foreign vessels from Canadian waters.
White livered halibut?	.** ;

speechtext:
I do not qnite understand mv hon. friend's desire to claim relationship with that kind of ' talibut,' but the government knows too that in the year before last there were some 38,000,000 pounds of halibut taken from Canadian waters by poachers, and it knows that this is due to the insufficient and inefficient fishery protection service, resulting in a failure to enforce the laws. The government knows that halibut banks in British Columbia are the best and almost the only halibut banks capable of profitable exploitation in the world to-day, and they realize, I believe, the necessity of protecting these banks. They have told us, and I believe that when they did so they acted sincerely, that they will improve that protection service. I have every reason to believe that the 'Joliffe,' a fast steamer, will be chartered pending the construction of a cruiser for the purpose of protecting our fisheries. In justice to the government I believe that they are grappling with the subject, and my hon. friend from Nanaimo notwithstanding, I am prepared to believe that their pledges about the protection of the fisheries and with regard to the productive development of the harbour of Vancouver, will be carried out by them. If my hon. friend (Mr. Smith) wants to keep himself posted on the pledges his government have made I can tell him that they are pledged to put a dredge in the harbour of Vancouver and I believe they will carry out that pledge, within the time stated, to the deputation that waited upon them recently. I am not one who would readily believe that the government has made these pledges for sinister and improper motives and that it does not intend to carry them out.
Now, it is true that on the public platform in Vancouver quite recently I did make reference to the idol before which my hon. friend from Nanaimo bows down. It was not an unholy reference; I spoke of the Colossus under whose huge legs my hon. friend from Nanaimo has been seeking and has at last apparently found a dishonourable political grave. I did make reference to that Colossus and I am sure that had my hon. friend (Mr. Smith) been present at that meeting he would admit that I had not transgressed the rules of political ethics or of decency, and I intend here and now to say exactly what I said on that platform. My hon. friend from Nanaimo will pardon me I am sure if I be not so imbued with reverence for his leader as to lose my sense of truth and of equity. At the Vancouver meeting I became reminiscent, and I examined the record of the Rt. Horn Sir Wilfrid Laurier on the question of the solidarity of the British empire and of Canada's desire to contribute to uphold that solidarity. I recalled the fact that on the 3rd of October, 1899 he declared in an interview with a correspondent of the* Globe,' his policy that not a man, not a gun could go from

Canada to South Africa. I remembered that from the Atlantic to the Pacific there was one great surging wave of enthusiasm in the hearts of the people and a desire that the Canadian boys should be allowed to go to South Africa. I remember that two days later, on the 5th of October, 1899, Sir Charles Tupper, on behalf of the Conservative party of Canada, wired Sir Wilfrid Laurier expressing the hope that a Canadian contingent would be allowed to go to Africa and assuring him of the loyal support of the Conservative party. I remembered that on the 7th of October, 1899, the ' Globe ' in an editorial declared for the policy of not a man and not a gun for South Africa until parliament had been summoned and had authorized it. I want my hon. friend from Nanaimo to remember the ground-swell of indignation that came up from the people of Canada on that occasion, and how, notwithstanding the technical and constitutional difficulties that bothered the Prime Minister, the Canadian boys did rush to the front on the way to death as to a festival. And, Sir, I say that when the sons of Canada did that they did more to bring about the birth of Canadian nationhood than all the blatant politicians that ever came from Nanaimo or anywhere else. I want to say here that I know exactly what my hon. friend (Mr. Smith) is appealing to when he charges this government with militarism and with spending $7,000,000 in fostering a military spirit in Canada. I know the little vote he is appealing to, and I want to tell the House that we know the hon. gentleman as a 40-per cent man in our country, because he succeeded in getting just about 40 per cent of the vote polled in his constituency.
Will my hon. friend permit me to ask him a question?
Why, yes.
Does he represent the majority of the vote in Vancouver?
I represent the second largest constituency in this Dominion of Canada, and I represent a bigger turnover at the last election than any single man in this parliament; that is what I represent.
As my hon. friend is making his attack personal to me
You made a personal attack.

I did not; I read his statements from the newspapers, and I never accused my hon. friend of making them. But my hon. friend (Mr. Cowan) knows that he sits in this House with 1,500 of a majority of the votes of Vancouver against him.

I sit in this House with a pluralty over every candidate against
me of 1,582 and I had an adverse majority to meet of 858 against me so that I represent a turnover of 2,440 votes. If any hon. gentleman can boast of a larger turnover than that in his constituency I am perfectly willing to take my seat and let him tell about it. When this sentiment in Canada in favour of standing at the back of the empire and preserving its solidarity was on the rise, where did we find the right hon. leader of the government? We found him saying: 'Canada is not menaced; I will not be stampeded; I will not act in a panic; I will not take any false step because of any false alarm.' It occurred to me, in looking over the records, that that same sentiment by that same gentleman has been expressed more than once in this House and on the public platforms of Canada. I recall that in 1907, when She right hon. gentleman, by entering into a treaty with Japan, inaugurated his policy of planting in British Columbia and in western Canada colonies of aliens who would always remain aliens, the aliens, quick to take advantage of that policy of his, came in thousands upon thousands into British Columbia, until in less than six months after the ratification of the treaty in January, 1907, there were no less than 8,125 Japanese army reservists and naval reservists landed in British Columbia to take possession of our fishing banks and our canneries. I remember again, when the influx of this Oriental horde was ,at its height, that the public feeling of resentment, especially in British Columbia, rose to fever height; and I remember that the right hon. gentleman, speaking to a meeting of manufacturers, I think in Toronto, again said in his spectacular way: 'I will not act in a panic; I will ponder; I will not take any false step, because of any false alarm.' That is the import of his words on that occasion; and I recalled at that time, as I recall now, that those army reservists and naval reservists had completely taken possession of the fishing grounds of British Columbia, which are to be the nurture ground of the sailors and officers of our future navy; and on a more recent occasion the same right hon. gentleman, after the greatest statesmen in the empire, the premier of Great Britain, the leader of the opposition, Mr. Balfour, and Mr. McKenna, had spoken weighty words as to the danger that threatened the empire-

Right here would my hon. friend allow me a question? Speaking of the Japanese, does my hon. friend believe that it is better to be on terms of friendship and amity and good will with Japan just now than it would be to be at war with her?

I believe that our first duty is to preserve our own self-respect, and I

believe that the way we should have preserved that self-respect would have been to have done as the home government asked us to do.
Denounce the treaty?
With dignity, reserve to oursely;es the right to control immigration from Japan.
How many Japanese are coming into Canada now?

I say I remember another occasion, when the solidarity of the empire was in question, and when the weighty men of the empire spoke weighty words. On the 16th of March last, Mr. Balfour said:
1 do not approach this problem, I can truly say to the House, in an alarmist spirit; but T have 'been forqed most reluctantly, not only against my wish, but against all the traditions by which British politicians and statesmen have been animated for generations. and now for the very first time in modern history, to declare that we are face to face with a situation so new, so dangerous, that it is very difficult for us fairly to realize all that it imports.
And the Premier of Great Britain, agreeing with Mr. Balfour, added 'that a contingency had arisen that menaced not only the supremacy of the empire at sea, but the independence of the nation itself.' Notwithstanding these weighty words by these weighty statesmen, again we find the right hon. leader of the government rise in his place in the House and declare: 'I will not be stampeded; I will not act in a panic; I will not make a false step because of a false alarm.' And I said to that audience, as I say here, that in the matter of the solidarity of the empire and Canada's desire to take part in upholding that solidarity, the only false alarm in the public life of Canada was the right hon. gentleman himself.
I also said something to that audience in regard to better terms. Now, I wish you to understand that we in British Columbia are human, and, like most men, when our rights are denied, we believe in a strong statement against the man who dares deny us our rights. Moreover, we believe that we have a just claim on the Dominion of Canada. It is deeply imbedded in the British sense of justice and fair play that every man who has a claim against an individual or a state will have a hearing before an independent and impartial tribunal. That is what we in British Columbia ask for. We do not ask you to believe in advance that our claim is well founded. We ask you simply to give us, in the name of common justice, a hearing before an independent and impartial tribunal, and we are satisfied; and I said then, what I am prepared to repeat, that Mr. COWAN.
any man who denies me or denies a province the right to have a claim which I or it considers a just claim, heard before an independent and impartial tribunal, that man, if a public man, is unworthy of his position as a public man, and is unworthy to be called a man.
Will my hon. friend permit me a question? Did he say that Sir Wilfrid Laurier was a white-livered traitor?
No, I will repeat exactly what I said, as nearly as I can remember.
