speechtext: It is my duty to point out that to ask an hon. member to repeat an expression which is out of order is asking him to repeat the offence, and I cannot allow him to do so.

I believe, Sir, that I can repeat exactly what I said, and that you will not be called on to rule the words out of order. What I said was that such white-livered treatment was unworthy of a public man or any man.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman is attributing to any member of this House a character of that description, he is using offensive words.

I wish to state that my purpose was to draw the attention of this House to the simple and material fact that we are denied the hearing of a claim which we believe to be just. All we ask is to be heard before an independent and impartial tribunal. I believe myself that when the right hon. the leader of this government realizes that position, when he realizes that the government, by its attitude, is denying us that hearing, his own innate sense of justice and right will lead him to change that attitude and give us the opportunity of pleading opr claim. If my hon. friend from Nanaimo (Mr. Ralph Smith) considers that I do not represent the public sentiment of my constituency upon the subject of better terms or on the attitude of the right hon. the leader of the government regarding the solidarity of the empire, I should be very grieved indeed to think that I do not represent the majority view of my constituency, and it will be one of my pleasures to contest with him or, if he chooses, with his leader whom he idolizes to such an extent, public opinion in the city of Vancouver; or if either of these gentlemen does not choose to take up the gauge of battle, possibly they may find some one courageous or bold enough, either resident or non-resident in Vancouver, to take it up in their place and on their behalf. I am here only because I believe I represent the healthy view of the people of Vancouver; and if I have fallen short of my duty, should any gentleman wish to contest public opinion in

Vancouver with me on that point, I want him to understand that the door is wide open for him to do so as soon as he wishes.

I thought that I had a fair majority in the last election, but it seems that my non. friend from Vancouver (Mr. Cowan) must have had a larger one. I wish to say a few words on the question before the House, which question also was under debate last week when we were discussing the woollen industry. In that discussion I heard some hon. members claiming to be farmers, others claiming to be labourers, and others claiming to have worked at certain industries during thirty or forty years, and all of them coming to the conclusion that more protection should be given our manufacturing industries. Much was said regarding the protection we should give the manufacturing element in this country, much was said regarding the protection we ought to give to the buildings themselves, the machinery in those buildings, the owners of those buildings, and also the stockholders in those companies. Much was said on behalf of their protection, but very little indeed on the labour side of the question. These hon. gentlemen seem to have forgotten that that is an element entitled to be seriously considered. For my part, I fail to see that our manufacturers are any poorer than they were ten or twelve years ago. I also know that time and again, especially in this very year, whenever the discussion of the budget is on, the Manufacturers' Association are particularly busy endeavouring to impress on the government the advisability of raising a large stone wall around the country-a wall so high that you cannot reach the top. But at the same time they want holes in it to let in their raw material and a wide door to allow labour to come in free. I only hope that our manufacturers, who are asking for higher protection, will seriously consider that whenever they are given protection of any kind, they should be at least willing to give a certain share of the profits allowed them by the tariff to the people who are producing their wealth.
Much has been said concerning the condition of the woollen industry. We had one hon. member telling us that he had been thirty years in that industry and imploring pathetically for more protection. But I believe that hon. gentleman is worth nearly a quarter of a million dollars. That industry must therefore pay very well or he would not have so much money. Again, take the cotton industry, and I have before me the report of the last royal commission held by Mr. King in the province of Quebec last year. It is proven by this report that, while that industry was asking for higher protection, it was impossible for it to produce enough cotton to meet the wants
of the Canadian people-there had to be importations in order to supply those wants. Even though two large establishments were built right at the doors of our city, they still could not make enough to supply the market. But I am sorry to say that, whenever the financial people get together, the only thing they seem to be looking for is to find means to cause this government to propose legislation to double their capital not in two years but in one year if possible. The manufacturers of this country are not satisfied to make ten, fifteen, or twenty per cent; they want more. And if, because of financial depression, such as we have had for the last eighteen months, they cannot make as much as they have been accustomed to make, the first thing they do is to cut down the wages of their employees. This is true not only of the cotton industry, but, so far as I can see, of all others throughout the country. If we are to have protection should we not have it for everything that will produce wealth for the people? I was pleased to hear the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Ralph Smith) speak on the subject of the militia. Every member of the House knows, I presume, that I am not very strongly in favour of militia. When the hon. member for Nanaimo asked that $3,500,000 of the budget of $7,000,000 for militia should be spent for the benefit of the farmers of the West and of the country generally, I believe he was right. As said by the hon. member for Nanaimo, we should protect a certain element in this country by trying, as far as possible, to keep our money in the channels of productive industry. I claim that the soldiers we have in this_country and the $7,000,000 a year that we are spending, would not enable us to defend even the old city of Quebec. It is not feather-bed soldiers that we want, but men who can fight.. I claim that there is no danger to be feared from outside; the worst enemy of this country that I can see is accumulated capital, the possession of which by a few reduces the rest of us virtually to the position of their subjects. This is our most dangerous enemy; this is the foe against which we should arm ourselves. Labour is not supposed to be at the mercy of capital. If we look at what is going on in England to-day we find the question ' discussed there whether capital is to be hired by labour or labour to be hired by capital. If we are not blind altogether, we can see that we are coming to the same position in this country. So long as we have men who try to breed a certain element and a strong element among our people, and are willing to come before this government and ask tariff or legislative favours, there exists an awful danger. Therefore, I hope that the

government instead of raising the tariff as asked by hon. members on the other side, will lower it and abolish the duties altogether in many instances.
We have been talking about expenses. I claim that it matters not so much what your expenses are, if the money is being spent for the good of the people. I would ask any hon. member of this House who has charge of the spending of money whether, in carrying on the industry in which he is engaged, he considers how much should be spent, or whether he considers only getting the good Teturn for that which is spent?
As to this question of tariff, when protection is asked for, it is always for the benefit of the poor labour people. The labour people are told: we are asking for high duties in order to protect you. But I say right here, let any member of this House prove to me that the labour people ever were protected. The benefits have come to the labour people when they were highly organized and able to protect themselves.
Hear, hear.
I am happy to hear the hon. member (Mr. Lalor) say ' Hear, hear.' I infer that he wants high protection for himself and not protection for labour.
I can tell the hon. gentleman that protection means high wages for the labouring people and artisans of this country. That is what it means in my factory and every other.

The manufacturers have less protection to-day than they had ten or twelve years ago. How is it, then, that they are paying their working people a little higher wages than they were then? They pay the labour people higher wages when they are forced to do so .and at no other time. The generosity of the manufacturers has no word to represent it in any language that I know; it is not explained in any grammar that I have ever seen or defined in any dictionary I have ever consulted. I have not learned anything about it in the twenty odd years that I have been in this movement. It is good enough to talk about in this House, but as we go from city to city observing the actual conditions, we do not find that generosity very much in evidence in any place that I know of. Any increase of wages has always been gained as the result of a struggle. Therefore, so far as the tariff is concerned I am not asking the government for a higher tariff, I am asking them to lower the tariff as much as possible, for we do not want high protection to the manufacturers and free trade in labour as has been the ease in the past. If these manufacturers are so anxious to provide work for our people, how is it that year after year the Manufacturers' Association are advertising throughout the whole world, you may say, that labourers of all Mr. VERVILLE.
kinds are in urgent demand in Canada? How is it that every year the Manufacturers' Association advertise, I might say throughout the world, that labour of all kinds is in urgent demand in Canada? If they are so anxious to give work to the unemployed, why do they try to make it appear that labour is scarce? Again, we find the Manufacturers' Association stating that workingmen are responsible for the present financial depression in the country. Will any hon. member say that the labouring men of Canada have not been as faithful in their work, that they have not worked just as hard the last two or three years as they ever did? Then how can they be responsible for the financial depression? But notwithstanding the financial depression, the stockholders must get their dividends, even on watered stock, and their dividends must be wrung out of the human flesh of the workingmen. Therefore I would urge upon this government, instead of raising the tariff, to lower it as much as possible, and I claim that by so doing they will benefit all the interests of Canada.

I consider that every man who has the honour of a seat in this House has a double obligation to perform; he has an obligation to his constituents who sent him here to represent what he believes to be their opinions on public questions, and he has an obligation to his fellow members in this House to do that as briefly as possible. I have listened with a great deal of interest to many of the speeches which have been delivered during this debate, and I was especially interested in observing the different positions taken by supporters of the government. The hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Verville) said among other things that he favoured tariff reduction as much as possible. Now, it is a little remarkable to me that an hon. gentleman who, I believe, sat in this House during the last parliament should so express himself. Last session the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Schaffner) moved a resolution to reduce the duty on agricultural implements from 17J to 10 per cent, and the hon. member who has just taken his seat, and the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Ralph Smith), who were both in this House, and every member on the Liberal side of the House, joined to vote that resolution down. It has been interesting to me to follow the arguments advanced by hon. gentlemen opposite; it is interesting to observe them labour to defend an expenditure which has risen to some $125,000,000. The position taken by hon. gentlemen supporting the government to-day is vastly different from that taken by the Liberal party previous to 1896, when, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, on every platform in Canada, they denounced in unmeasured terms an expenditure of $38,000,000, while

to-day we find them labouring to defend an expenditure of $125,000,000.
I agree with much that has been said this evening by my hon. friend from Nanaimo (Mr. Smith), and I think that many on this side of the House will agree with much that he has said. I think that the Conservative party in this House, as well as the Liberal party, favour a proper expenditure of money, an expenditure that will increase our transportation facilities and benefit the country. But where the Conservative party differs from hon. gentlemen opposite, is that they condemn expenditure which, in their judgment, are improper, while hon. gentlemen opposite are ready to back up any expenditure proposed by the government no matter how indefensible it may be. For instance, the hon. member for Nanaimo is today finding fault with the government for spending money on militia and defence; he says that an expenditure of $7,000,000 for that purpose is unjustifiable, that the money should not be used in that way. But what has been the course of that hon. gentleman for the last four or five years that he has been in this House? Every session, when six or seven million dollars has been voted by parliament for militia purposes, the hon. gentleman has supported that vote. This session he did not raise his voice against an expenditure of $7,000,000 for militia purposes after all the money was appropriated, and now he comes forward and raises a howl about it. I think we might characterize his course on this question as one of those political spasms to which he referred. It is interesting to note that while the hon. member advocates free coal, the hon. member for Cape Breton North (Mr. McKenzie) advocates a higher duty on coal; that while some Liberal members advocate a reduction of the duty on different articles, other Liberal members advocate an increased duty on various articles. The policy of the Conservative party since 1879 has been known as the National Policy, the N. P. The Liberal policy, if we may judge by the diverse opinions expressed by Liberal members, might be properly termed the M. P., that is the Mixed Policy, a policy which is applicable to the condition of every constituency which they represent. We find the present government going down to Nova Scotia and telling the people that they will not touch the duty on coal, or if they do, that they will increase it; and going up to British Columbia and assuring the people that the proper thing to do is to reduce the duty on coal. We find that every Liberal member who gets up in this House to speak, whether it is the hon. member for Nanaimo who advocates free coal, he gets applause from the government benches; whether it is the hon. member for Cape Breton who advocates an increased duty on coal, he also gets applause from the government benches;
or whether it is the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark), who is prepared to advocate anything that comes into his head, he is also applauded. I was particularly struck with some of the arguments, if I might dignify them with the name of arguments, advanced by my philosophical friend from Red Deer. The hon. member for Red Deer said among other things that the credit of Canada was to be judged by our answer to the question, 'What is our faith in Canada? It strikes me that the credit of Canada is to be judged rather by the faith of the other fellow, who is the creditor of Canada. Another argument advanced by the hon. member for Red Deer was that we spend what we get, and he says that we get our money from the increase of our trade. I might ask him, 'How do we get an increased income from increased trade if it is not by means of duties imposed by this government on trade? The hon. member for Red Deer has advanced the peculiar doctrine in this House to-day, that we in Canada must regard, and should regard, any increase in Canada's expenditure as a token of Canada's prosperity, and as a token as well of the administrative abilitv of the present administration.
I submit that of all the peculiar arguments that have been advanced in this House of parliament by any member, let alone the member who claims and professes to be somewhat of a philosopher, this is, to my mind, the most peculiar. The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) has a great admiration for the Minister of Finance. He admires the steady persistence shown by the Minister of Finance to the requests of the manufacturers, but he has forgotten that in this present budget the only change made was one in the interest of manufacturers and asked for by manufacturers. Has he likewise forgotten that the Minister of Finance could not resist the appeals of the manufacturers of iron and steel in this country, but that he gave way to their appeals and that this government has granted, since 1896, in bounties to manufacturers of iron, steel and various other commodities over $16,000,000 of the public money? The hon. member for Red Deer supports that sort of thing. That is a style of protection which he applauds although he is in theory an ardent free trader. That is the great trouble with that hon. gentleman and with a great many hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House; in theory they are free traders while in practice they are protectionists. There is one more reference that I desire to make to one of the statements made by the hon. member for Red Deer and that is the expression which fell from his lips that he had the fullest sympathy with any aspirations for true economy. It was a beautiful sentence, beautifully expressed-that he had the fullest sympathy with any aspirations for true economy. Yet,

the hon. member for Red Deer stood up in this House and gave his support to the throwing away of $1,000,000 of the public money for the Aylesworth ditch.
Will the hon. gentleman tell me the date when I stood up in this House and voted for that ditch?
If I have mis-stated anything in reference to the hon. member for Red Deer I will be very sorry. I will ask him if he was in the House at the time.
My hon. friend made a definite statement purporting to be a fact about myself. I asked him the authority upon which he stated as a fact what was not a fact.

They will say: 'Ha, ha.'

We have a good many policies advocated by the Liberal party in the Dominion of Canada. We have had tariff for revenue only, we have had free trade as it is in England, we have had unrestricted reciprocity or commercial union, a policy which one of the ablest men that the Liberal party ever produced in this country could not back up and on account of which he left the Liberal party. He believed that the leaders of the Liberal party at that time, in advocating that policy, and in allying themselves with men like Wyman, Farrer and other annexationists, were making the first move towards giving this country away to the people across the line. We have had various policies advanced and advocated by the liberal party, and to-day we have a policy which we might properly call a mixed policy, because it seems to me to apply to any constituency and to any member of this House if he is on the Liberal benches whether he be in favour of free trade or

in favour of protection. It is an accommodating policy and to that extent it deserves to be styled a mixed policy. In 1893 there was a convention held in the city of Ottawa to which Liberals were called from all parts of Canada. That convention was representative of the Liberal party of Canada. At that convention the platform laid down was that on which the Liberal party appealed to the country in the elections following in 1896. In one of the planks of that platform they stated that the Liberal party viewed with alarm the increase in the national debt. They seem to view with the utmost complacency an increase of $60,317,999 to the public debt in the last two years. In 1896 the right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) expressed himself in these words:
The expenditure has grown until the people are unable to bear it. I promise you that if you put our party in power we will reduce that annual expenditure by two or three millions of dollars.
We hold as individuals, one with another, that a man should be as good as his word. That is the test that we have in sizing up a man. If his word is good he is good for anything but if his word is no good the man himself is considered no good. The same test should be applied to governments. If the Liberal party made these solemn promises in 1896 to the people of Canada they should have kept them. If these men made these promises knowing at the time that it would be impossible in a growing country like Canada to decrease the annual expenditure then they made them for the purpose of wilfully deceiving the people. If they made these promises believing they could carry them out, then I maintain it is up to them to explain why they have not carried them out. The promise made by the Prime Minister in 1896 was supplemented by a promise made by Sir Richard Cartwright. He said that an expenditure of $38,000,000 or $40,000,000 was monstrous, and that when the United States mustered a population of 20,000,000 their expenditure was barely $22,000,000. If that argument of Sir Richard Cartwright were well founded, then according to that basis of calculation the present expenditure of the Dominion government is sufficient for a population of 110,000,000 people in this country. The people of Canada took the Liberal party at their word and placed them in power, and the right hon. the Prime Minister who pledged his word to reduce the then expenditure by two millions or three millions a year, now views with complacency an annual expenditure of $125,000,000, and he even expresses his pride in a Minister of Finance who can spend that amount of money and in a minister of Public Works who can throw away $1,000,000 into the Aylesworth ditch, and who

can permit the looting of the public treasury by his bosom friend to the extent of nearly $36,000 of the people's money.
Now, Sir, I wish to refer very briefly to the tariff plank in the Liberal platform of 1893. The Liberals stated at that time that the tariff should be reduced to the needs of honest, economical, and efficient government. No one in this House will claim that the tariff has been reduced to any such extent, and the natural conclusion is that the needs of this government require three or four times as much as was required by the Conservative government, or else, that this government is neither honest, nor economical, nor efficient. You can have your choice of whichever it is. I will not take up the time of the House by referring in detail
Hear, hear.

I can, however, tell these hon. gentlemen opposite that I am going to take up just as much time of the House as I think necessary to make out my argument. I shall not now refer in detail to the various expressions used by Liberal politicians from 1893 to 18% in reference to the tariff. The right hon. the Prime Minister said that if the Liberals were successful they would cut the head off protection and trample on its body. Well, protection is a pretty lively corpse at the present day in Canada. Sir Richard Cartwright declared that the policy of the Liberal party was death to protection; Sir Louis Davies said that protection was a system accursed by God and man, and the Hon. Wm. Paterson nailed his banner to the mast and joined in the procession with the motto:	We declare for freedom
of trade. But, after the Liberal party came to power he tacks on to that motto the words:	Except in biscuits. Well, Sir,
notwithstanding all these pledges made by Liberal statesmen of that day we still have the same line of custom houses and an increased staff of customs officials collecting pretty much the same duties as were collected previous to 1896. In reference to tariff and taxation I want to reiterate the statement made by the hon. member for North Toronto-and it is a statement which has not been denied by any Liberal member-that the taxation of the people in 1896 was $5.46 per head of the population and in 1908 it was $11 per head of the population. Let me say further that if the Conservative government from 1887 to
1896	had exacted a similar amount of taxation to that levied by the Liberals from
1897	to 1908 the Conservative government would not only not have increased the debt of this country but they would have reduced it by some $120,000,000. Or if you like you can put it the other way: If the Liberals had not increased the taxation to meet the ever growing expenditure they
would have added over $150,000,000 to the debt of this country. Hon. gentlemen opposite are very fond of referring to the conditions previous to 1896 and they tell _us that the present time is one of financial stress and trade depression. But, Sir, in the period from 1890 to 1894 commercial depression was world wide and Canada came through it better than any other country in the world. In support of my statement that trade depression was world wide between 1890 and 1894 I would point out that the falling off in exports from Great Britain amounted to $235,000,000 and the falling off in her imports to $60,000,000; in the United States there was a falling off in exports amounting to $140,000,000 and a falling off in imports amounting to $170,000,000; in Australia there was a falling off in exports amounting to $95,000,000 and a like decrease in the value of imports; in France there was a falling off in exports to the amount of $95,000,000 and in imports to the extent of $65,000,000; in Germany there was a falling off in exports of $40,000,000 and in imports of $50,000,000. The depression felt in Canada at that time was shared in by all the great commercial countries in the world, but in Canada, while her import trade remained stationary her export trade increased by $17,000,000; her earnings increased by $46,000,000^ .her railways increased by 2,700 miles; her coasting trade by 2,700,000 tons; her imports of raw material doubled, her exports of manufactured articles increased by 35 per cent and her exports of agricultural products by 65 per cent. And I want to say that the Conservative government at that time, realizing that it was a time of stress, adopted the wise course of reducing the annual expenditure and besides that they reduced taxation. Let me point out that in 1890 the Conservative government took taxes off the necessaries of life amounting to over half a million dollars, that in 1891 they took the duty off raw sugar and reduced the duty on refined sugar, thus saving to the people from 1891 to 1895 nearly $20,000,000 in that way alone. In 1894 they' followed up their wise policy and they made a general reduction in taxes amounting to upwards of one and a half million dollars. This reduction of taxes, this lifting of the burden from the people at that time was the policy of the Conservative party. I hold Sir, that in comparing the tariff of to-day with the Conservative tariff of 1896 we must take into consideration the general increase in the cost of goods which amounts to from 30 per cent to 50 per cent. It is true there have been reductions made by the Liberal government on some things; they claim for instance that the duty on various articles of iron have been lowered. But I submit that it is fair, in considering that statement, to consider also the fact that while

they reduced the duties on certain manufactured articles, they gave in bounties to manufacturers of iron, steel and other things, over $16,300,000. That is just as much a form of protection as the placing of a specific or ad valorem duty on an article imported.
Very much has been made of the fact that trade has very largely increased since 1896, which I am very pleased to admit; it was only to be expected that it would increase. But of the eighteen leading countries named in volume 1 of the report of the Department of Trade and Commerce, Argentina was the only country whose percentage of imports during the last decade was greater than that of Canada; but there is a very great difference in the way the trade of the two countries is balanced. I find that the percentage of increase of imports in Argentina in the last decade was 190'84 and the percentage of increase of exports was 192-78, thus showing not only a large increase in the total volume of trade, but a favourable balance of trade as well. Canada's percentage of increase of imports in the last decade was 178-59; but her percentage of increase of exports was only 75 -5, showing a very large adverse balance of trade.	Allow me also to call
your attention to this fact, that of the eighteen principal countries mentioned six show a favourable condition of trade, so far as it is indicated by imports and exports; seven show practically the same percentage of increase of exports as of imports; and of the other five, the adverse balance of trade is far greater in the case of Canada than in the case of any of the others, For the year ending the 31st of March, 1908, Canada's imports for home consumption amounted to $351,879,955, and her exports of domestic merchandise amounted to $246,960,968; in other words, Canada bought nearly $105,000,000 worth more from other countries than she sold to other countries. This means that our imports amount to $52.87 and our exports $37.10 per head of the _ population. Now, I submit that if a business man or a farmer, year after year, continued to buy from others more than he sold to others, there could be only one result, namely, that he would be obliged to borrow in order to carry on his business; and what applies to the individual applies in a larger sense to the country as a whole. The balance of trade in 1908 was unfavourable to Canada to the extent of nearly $105,000,000. In 1896, while the total volume of our trade was very much less than it was in 1908, the balance of trade in Canada's favour was $7,600,000. Hon. gentlemen opposite, I know, profess to make light of this balance of trade; but I observe that when they are referring to our trade with Great Britain, they seem to take a great deal of pleasure in the fact that we. are exporting to Great Britain more than we are import-Mr. EDWARDS.
ing from Great Britain. Now, I think that our trade relations with Great Britain, so far as the figures show, are -very satisfactory. In 1896 Canada bought from Great Britain over $32,000,000 worth and sold her over $66,000,000 worth, showing a balance of trade in our favour of over $34,000,000. In 1898 Canada bought from Great Britain $64,000,000 worth and sold to Great Britain $104,000,000 worth, or a balance of trade in favour of Canada of $40,000,000. In my judgment that represents a very satisfactory state of trade as between this country and Great Britain. But if we regard that state of trade as satisfactory, so far as Canada is concerned, what must we think of the state of trade revealed by the figures of Canada's trade with the United States? In 1896 our trade with the United States showed an adverse balance of $17,000,000, and in 1908 we sold to the United States $96,900,000 worth, and bought from the United States $214,000,000 worth, showing an adverse balance of trade in the neighbourhood of $118,000,000.
Now, I wish to express the opinion, which I shall endeavour to back up with figures, that the unsatisfactory condition of our trade relations with the United States is largely due to the unwise, and, if I may be permitted to say so, the unfair policy maintained by this government. I am not going to claim to be a farmer. That is not my profession. I represent a farming constituency, and have lived all my life in the country amongst farmers; and I have had an opportunity to come into contact with them and to ascertain pretty fairly what their views are. In 1908 Canada imported from the United States of animals living, $2,000,000 worth, of which $1,611,000 worth were dutiable and $453,000 worth were free. Of grains of all kinds we imported from the United States over $14,000,000 worth, of which $8,250,000 worth were free. Of breadstuffs we imported from the United States over $15,000,000 worth, of which over $8,250,000 worth were free. Of fruits we imported nearly $6,000,000 worth; of butter, cheese, eggs, lard and meat we imported $3,612,334 worth; and of vegetables we imported $851,451 worth. Now, I wish to state to the House why I think the tariff between Canada and the United States is unfair to the Canadian market. We imported into Canada from the United States in 1908, 6,428 horses, the value of which, as represented in the blue-books, was $1,254,744, and we sent to the United States that same year 3,616 horses, the value of which was $901,350.
Permit me very briefly to compare the Canadian tariff on horses with that of the United States. The United States charge Canadians a duty of $30 on all horses valued under $150 each, and 25 per cent on horses exceeding that value. Our tariff charges on American horses brought into this coun-

try 25 per cent, if a horse is worth $150, and $12.50 on horses valued at $50 and under. You see how that works out. Suppose a Canadian farmer has four horses to spare and sends them to the American market. One of them he values at $100, the other at $75, and two colts at $50 and $30 respectively. What duty has he to pay? Before he can get them into the American market, he must pay a duty of $30 each, or a total duty of $120. But suppose an American farmer sends into the Canadian market four horses of exactly the same kind, what duty will he have to pay? On the $100 horse, he will have to pay $25; on the $75 horse, $18.75; and on each of the colts $12.50, so that he pays a duty of $68.75 on these animale while the Canadian farmer has to pay a duty of $120. I submit that that is manifestly unfair and unjust to Canadian farmers: and when we take into account the fact that the United States sent into Canada last year 6,428 horses, valued at $1,254,704, we must see that a portion of that was deliberately taken out of the pockets of Canadian farmers.
Let me carry the comparison further and give a statement with regard to hay and different other articles. We allow the Americans to ship hay into this country on paying a duty of $2 per ton, whereas Canadians must pay a duty of $4 per ton on hay which they send into the United States. Is there anything fair in that? I think not. The United States sent into this country last year 11,258 tons of hay, and I do not believe they would have sent us that much if our duty had been the same as theirs.
