Earlier in the session we were told by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) that the drawback to agricultural productions in this country was the slipshod methods of our farmers, their lack of industry, and the lack of labour necessary in the carrying out of farming operations. That was the opinion expressed by the hon. minister of ^ the farmers of this country, and that opinion I would respectfully com-

not to kill outright, even people with a most hearty stomach.
There is one point brought out by the member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) which I desire to deal with. He is unable to conceive how it comes that the present administration having accumulated surpluses up to $94,000,000 and having spent that money, they should not be in a position to account to him for their use. I realize his great embarrassment in having to deal with surpluses, he, among all others, who has always had deficits on hand.
Let me show you briefly the actual difference in the political status of the two parties who have been contending for power. When the Conservatives came to power in 1878, the total assets of Canada amounted to $34,595,499.05. In 1896, these gentlemen were driven out of power by the verdict of the people. In the meantime, they had brought the assets of Canada up to $67,220,103.96; that is to say, they had increased them by $32,624,004.91 in the space of 18 years. However, they had brought the debt during that period up to $118 000,000. After deducting from the above amount the $32,500,000 of assets to their credit, there remains a net increase of the debt during those 18 years of $85,500,000, for which the Conservative party is responsible.
We came to power in 1896, when the assets of Canada, as I said a moment ago, aggregated $67,220,103.96. By 1909, we had increased that amount to $130,246,298, that is an increase, during those twelve of Liberal government, of $63,026,194.04. Now, according to the official report of the Finance Department, the debt under the Liberal government has increased by $65,463,427.07. But the assets represent $63,026,194.04. Therefore, the net Tncrease of the debt for which we are responsible amounts only to $2,437,233.03.	_	,
The member for North Toronto inquired the other day how it was that having had surpluses amounting to $94,000,000, we should not he in a position to account for them. Let him consider the net increase of the debt, and he will find out that the difference in round figures, amounts to only $2,500,000.	,
Regarding the use that has been made of the surpluses, let my hon. friend refer to the official reports and he will see that the National Transcontinental has already cost to this country $52,574,131; that about $8,000,000 have been expended on our canals-I am speaking from memory-that the better terms granted to the provinces, account for $3,000,000; if we add to the above several other items aggregating to about $12,000,000, it will be seen that of the $94,000,000 of accumulated surpluses, $75,000,000 have thus been employed.

I will stop at that, and I will impose no more figures upon the House.
Now, Mr. Speaker, there is in this House an extraordinary man, a man without the like of him; he is generally referred to as the best debater of this country. But he also excels in some other ways, he can accommodate himself with a marvellous versatility to the exigencies of the most heterogeneous situations. I am alluding to the hon. member for North Toronto. When the hon. gentleman sits to your right, Mr. Speaker, he is the most persistent accumulator of deficits. When he sits to your left, he wages war unceasingly on the surpluses of the government.	.
He is an extraordinary man in another direction yet. Twelve or thirteen years ago, he delivered a splendid speech-of which we hear a repetition every year. I refer to his criticism of the budget speech. Those who hear that speech for the first time are found to say: What an orator! Those who hear it for the second time, say: What a repeater. But those who hear it for the fourth or fifth time-and that is the case of those of us who have long enjoyed a seat in this House-are hound to say: That gentleman sings always the same tune; he is a grinding organ.
I would dislike to make these remarks in his absence, but as this same speech comes back to us regularly about Easter time, quite innocent people say that the ex-manager of the Union Trust, the friend of the Independent Foresters, is about to repent. On the other hand, those who do not know more about the ritual than about the dogma, say: He has a sermon in store for us, but it will not be on the last sufferings of the Saviour.
The hon. member for North Toronto has made a crime to the government for having borrowed money recently, at a different rate than the one they had obtained some time before. It is of no use to argue on this point, for everybody knows that when one goes to the money markets of the world to float a loan he must submit to the financial conditions of the market, for the time being.
The hon. member has taunted the hon. Finance Minister with having changed his views on the political questions concerning this country. He has recalled that Sir Richard Cartwright has always been true to his colours and so with Sir John A. Macdonald. The political convictions of Sir John A. Macdonald do not concern me, but I can say of Sir Richard Cartwright that if during the five years he has been Finance Minister in a Liberal administration, he has never changed his views on the political question of the day, the reason was that there was no necessity for him to do so, his task being confined to relieve the country of the evil effects of the preceding administration.

Moreover, it is an accepted truism that asses only never change their views, for the good reason that they have none. In my opinion, a statesman is bound to conform his views to the needs of the country, without considering if in doing so he has to modify his former views.
The country having been left in a depressed condition by the Conservative party in 1896, it was but natural that the succeeding government should gradually modify the existing fiscal policy, so as to bring about the prosperity that we presently enjoy.
The other night, the hon. member for North Toronto found fault with the hon. Finance Minister for having charged' to capital account the expenses incurred in connection with the bounties on iron and steel. In our time, said the hon. gentleman, these bounties were charged to current accounts. I do not doubt it, because under the former administration these industries were almost at a standstill and the bounties amounted to a mere triffle.
Furthermore, the hon. member for North Toronto is not consistent in his statements. He complains about the heavily increasing expenditures, notwithstanding the fact that in Prince Edward Island he advocated an expenditure of $50,000,000 for the construction of a tunnel. Later on he made a strong plea in favour of the construction of Dreadnoughts. But his most stupendous contradiction is when he stands in this House and denounces the construction of the National Transcontinental Railway as a crime.	.
If he is in earnest, if his friends are in earnest, if they sincerely wish to do something for the defence of the Empire, they cannot suppress the fact that the contraction of this Transcontinental Railway exclusively on Canadian territory, is the most patriotic and imperialistic scheme that could be conceived.
Let us suppose that England should be called upon for the protection of her interests in the Far East, to transfer her forces, her whole army, together with contingents from Australia. New Zealand, South Africa, India and even France, nothing would equal the advantages to be derived from the transportation facilities afforded by that magnificent line of railway.
The hon. member for North Toronto favours the construction of the battleships It is not an easy thing to express a decided opinion on this question at the present moment, nevertheless let us take the figures by the hon. member himself, who stated that the construction of the National Transcontinental will cost the enormous sum of $180,000,000. Now it is an admitted fact, 151
that the construction of a single Dreadnought costs $10,000,000. So by the construction of the Transcontinental Railroad we are contributing towards the defence of the Empire, the equivalent of eighteen Dreadnoughts. That proposition ^ cannot be assailed. Those who are urging the defence of the empire, if they are m earnest, must withstand all criticism concerning the construction of that railway. There is no more effective way of contributing to the defence of the empire.
What is this Dreadnought policy aimed at ? At putting Canada in the throep of the most pronounced form of imperialism. For my part, Mr. Speaker, I say it from the bottom of my heart and without boasting-I am an anti-imperialist. First of all,
I am a son of Canada.
In what situation would we be in acceding to the construction of Dreadnoughts, which, after all would be the exclusive property of the English nation ?
(Translation.) Will my hon. friend allow me a question ?
(Translation.) Certainly.
(Translation.) When has the hon. member for North Toronto advocated the construction of Dreadnoughts?

(Translation.) I am sorry for my hon. friend, but it is quite evident that he did not bother himself much with the reading of that speech of the hon. member for North Toronto. It is in the last part of his speech that_ the hon. member advocated the construction of battleships. I was asking in what situation would we find ourselves in acceding to the construction of these Dreadnoughts, which would be, after all, the exclusive property of the Engilsh nation? We have been enticed to imperialism on every hustings, in England, in Canady and in this House. Have we not yet, on the Order Paper a resolution of the hon. member for Victoria-Haliburton (Mr. Hughes) teeming with the most fervid imperialism of the hon. gentlemen on the other side? 'In cauda venenum.'
Would not that pronounced form of_ imperialism create a most anomalous condition of things for a considerable portion of our pooulation ? Let us suppose that one day the land and naval forces of England and Germany clash against each other. If we have allowed ouTselves to be enticed into imperialism, we are in duty bound to fight for the empire. What right have we to ask the Germans, the Italians, that have become naturalized citizens of this country, to fight against Germany or Italy ? If these citizens of Canada, being in such an awkward position, should refuse to draw the sword against their kinsmen, should they be declared rebels and traitors ? If, on the other hand, they go to war, do we not



ask them to become murderers and fratra-cides ? In the first case, they are to be shot as rebels ; in the second case, they are to be disgraced for fighting against their own blood.
I may be allowed to state in all frankness that I am neither English, nor French; I am nothing else than a Canadian; I would not give a token to return under French domination. But for nothing on earth would I see my fellow countrymen of the province of Quebec being called upon to take up arms against the French army. These are my sentiments on this question.
Moreover, we have no right to decide about the future. The future does not belong to us. A great poet has said "The future belongs to God." It is true; but the expectations of the future are ours; it is our duty to transmit them as an inheritance to those that will come after us. It would be a crime, an outrage, to deprive them of that inheritance. We have no right, be it in the form of a Dreadnought policy, or in the form of imperialism, to imperil the future of this country in entering into a scheme of the consequences of which we know nothing. We have a perfect right to have expectations and to hope that they will be realized in the future; but no matter what that future has in store for our country, we have no right to dispose of that future.
I do not think I can be accused of being disloyal for giving expression to these sentiments; as I have just said, I would not give a token to return under French domination. I believe that our country ought to be proud of the present status. I love the British Empire that has given Canada more liberty than this country had ever enjoyed before; I love that mighty Empire oyer which the sun never sets; I love the king of the United Kingdom, the worthy successor of the most admirable woman that for centuries has sat on a British throne. But there is another country that I cannot forget; a country to which God has given the dimensions of a continent, a country bounded on both sides by the Oceans, a country which has as neighbour on the one side the greatest republic in the world, and which on the other side is bordered by the mysteries of unknown seas. All our ancestors have proven it. That country is yours, Mr. Speaker, it is mine, it is the country of us all. It is the country of the English, who on that soil so gallantly and gloriously fought us; it is the country of the French Canadians who opened it to civilization and who, themselves also fought some immortal fights. That country, we all know, is Canada.
I fail to see what advantage we could be, for the defence of the empire, by building Dreadnoughts, or by throwing ourselves Mr. GLADU.
into exaggerated imperialism. England has got nothing to fear from us-I speak of Canadians of all races and of all creeds. Every time that her flag has been threatened on Canadian soil, every time an audacious hand has been stretched towards that same flag, the French and English Canadians stepped forth for her defence. Let us open history. In 1774-75, Canadians kept the British flag flying on the citadel of Quebec. In 1812, de Salaberry and his companions gain immortal fame in history at Chateau-guay. In 1870, during the Fenian raid Canadians again stood by the flag. In 1885, that flag was threatened once more. On that occasion, we were face to face with our own kin; and yet, it was for the defence of that same flag, and as loyal subjects of the British empire, we did not hesitate to crush the rebellion. And even now, when I come to more recent times, the blood of our compatriots is still reeking on the battle fields of the African soil.
What benefit, what privileges would we find in a more intimate union with the empire? What would be the profit to England? Absolutely none. Let us then remain as we are, loyal British subjects. The money we have to spend, let us spend it for the general good of Canada; that our country may attain that prosperity and greatness to which it is entitled, and some day perhaps become one of the finest and greatest countries on the face of the globe. I do not believe, a Canadian, who Teally loves his country, and wishes to show his love for it, could possibly form any other dreams.

Mr. Speaker, without making any such nice phrases as those we have just heard from the member for Yamaska, I will be satisfied to simply congratulate him. He has spoken to us in an ornate tongue, but I do not wish to dwell upon it any longer, and I come at once to the point which he particularly insisted upon, and that is imperialism.
Answering the remarks made by the hon. gentleman, I will read, not in full, but partly only, the resolution adopted by this House, and compare it with that submitted by the member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster).
The member for North Toronto proposed as follows:
That in view of her great and varied resources, or her geographical position and national environments, and of that spirit of self help and self respect which alone befits a strong and growing people, Canada should no longer delay in assuming her proper share of the responsibility and financial burden incident to the suitable protection of her exposed coast line and great seaports.
To that resolution an amendment was brought forward by the right hon. leader
APRIL 22. 1909 [DOT]
of the government. And what does this last resolution of the right hon. gentleman contain? I read a portion only of its conclusions :
The House will cordially approve of any recessary expenditure designed to promote the speedy organization of a Canadian naval service in co-operation with and in close relation to the imperial navy, along the lines suggested by the Admiralty at the last Imperial Conference, and in full sympathy with the view that the naval supremacy of Britain is essential to the security of commerce, the safety of the Empire and the peace of the world.	_	_
The House expresses its firm conviction that whenever the need arises the Canadian people will be found ready and willing to make any sacrifice that is required to give to the Imperial authorities the most loyal and hearty co-operation in every movement for the maintenance of the integrity and the honour of the Empire.
Really, on hearing the bon. member for Yamaska express so strongly to-night that frightful theory of imperialism, I am inclined to believe that he is no staunch supporter of the government. Does he wish to strike his chief in the face? I cannot bring myself to imagine he would have that courage. I will insist no longer on that question; I think the most appropriate answer is found in that part of ' Hansard ' which I have just quoted. I have, also, no intention whatever of defending the hon. member for North Toronto. I know he is well able to defend himself, and will, therefore, leave the matter in his hands.
The hon. member for Yamaska has told us of the bounties paid by the Conservatives when in poweT. The bounties paid during that administration were far from considerable, because the Conservative party had quite different ideas as to national politics, and did not give the bounties any great attention. National industries were encouraged in quite another manner. This was perhaps a bad policy, but such was its policy, and it is not here the place nor is it the time to discuss it. Bounties then could not have had any great influence in equilibrating its budget.
My hon. friend has stated that the hon. member for North Toronto, during his term as Minister of Finance, could show nothing but yearly deficits. That assertion is completely in opposition with the facts, and one has only to open the blue-books, to find not only the refutation of the accusation, but also to get proof that the hon. member foT North Toronto was able to show an occasional surplus.
On the other hand, what is the substance and material of the surplus of which the present ministers are so boastful ? If one follows the easy methods of the Minister of Finance, it seems to me quite any easy matter to have a surplus. I do not know if the secret is one of his own invention, 151J
but according to his ideas, it is sufficient to capitalize the revenue. He does not spend public money, he capitalizes it. It is according to those ideas that he capitalized the $6,424,000 sunk with the Quebec bridge. Strange capital, I must say. _
The hon. minister pays to certain industries bounties amounting to $2,787,354, and in his mind, this is also a capital, although the government have assumed these obligations by means of a law obliging them to pay the bounties ; yet, at the end of the year, the minister does not hesitate to capitalize that also. The same system applies to the grants to the railways ; again my hon. friend includes them in his capital. Following that plan right through, he will probably end by capitalizing the expenses of the public servants. Putting all that to the credit of capital, he, of course easily finds a surplus. Really, I think the Minister of Finance should have his invention patented.
But they tell us he simply borrowed the system from his predecessor, the hon. member for North Toronto, who was minister before him. If it be true, I say he was quite wrong in doing so. But I do not believe that he, a proud and dignified Liberal, could possibly make use of methods so decidedly Tory in their essence.
The Minister of Finance has been in power for the last thirteen years, and with all his progressive ideas, he has not been able so far to change that wrong method. He might have invited his colleague the Minister of Marine (Mr. Brodeur) and imported a book-keeper from New York, who could have taught him a new system of book-keeping. If it be true that the Conservative party was the first to imagine and apply the theory of capitalization of expenses, the Conservatives greatly deserved to be thrown over and become the opposition, and if the Liberals act in a similar manner, they are equally deserving of a similar treatment, and should pass into the opposition as quick as possible.
Simple minded and innocent, I had thought that a sum of money could be converted into capital when that sum of money represented a real and solid value, and I said to myself; now here is a farmer who, as a result of strict economy, has saved a sum of $1,000. He takes that money, builds a barn on his farm; he is not impoverished thereby, he simply puts his cash into a building and adds so much to the value of his property ; he can in all justice charge that sum of $1,000 to his credit and capital account. But the Minister of Finance acts differently, he capitalizes all the money he spends. The principle is a false one, and the method quite wrong, when applied to financial dealings.
A government who builds a railway will

capitalize its real value, because it is equivalent to cash or credit on hand. But certainly that cannot be said of the $6,400,000 of the Quebec bridge, which he buried in the bottom of the St. Lawrence. The old members of this House know and understand the meaning of these surpluses the Minister of Finance speaks of, but the new members do not know, neither do the public, and all this is likely to be misleading to the people, the creditors, and to the Minister of Finance himself.
There seems to be very little chance of an understanding in this matter of accounting, but there is a wonderful understanding as to the frightful proportions of the public debt. The public debt has in the last two years increased by $46,000,000. We are living on loans. We have long term and medium term loans; we have also temporary loans which, I might say, are on the weekly payment or instalment system. Here we find a condition of things that requires prompt attention. And yet, I believe we are extravagant in the administration of our affairs. And that is the point I had most particularly intended to develop. We are extravagant in the salaries we pay to the Government officials, we are quite exaggerating in the extent and largeness of certain salaries. We are also sometimes exaggerating in the smallness of some other salaries paid to the small and humble servants in the public service. This was brought to my mind the other day, when the hon. Postmaster-General Mr. Lemieux, brought for- [ ward his bill in connection with the salaries paid in his department. We insisted on this side of the House, that he should grant certain postmen, mail carriers and other humble post office officials, a sum sufficient to permit them to live.
The hon. minister protested, saying: 'Gentleman, what you are asking from me represents a large amount of money, and I desire and so do my colleagues, to practice strict economy.'
I felt inclined to rise and say to him: 'Gentlemen of the Government, if you wish to practice economy, I can only congratulate you; but for mercy's sake do not try and practice it on the backs of the starving, but rather on the heads of those who gluttonously feed on favouritism. There is more to reap on the salaries of five, six, nine and ten thousand dollars, than there is to pare and clip from the salaries of five and six hundred dollars.'
I did not even open my mouth, reserving my right to return to the subject when The opportunity offered itself; and I believe it offers itself now. I notice that the Minister of Finance does away entirely, in his estimates for 1909-10, with an amount of $22,581,458. I hope that this saving will not be too much at the expense of those earning small salaries, and that the Post-Mr. NANTEL.
master General who has obtained a surplus, an effective surplus, will see that these people do not suffer in consequence. It should not be inferred from my reference to the hon. Postmaster General that my criticism is aimed specially at him. In the first place, I have no ill feeling towards any of the hon. gentlemen occupying the treasury benches, and this is particularly the case as regards the Postmaster General. I have no intention of criticising his department; on the contrary, were I to follow my inclination, and were it not for fear of annoying so modest a man, I would say that if there is a minister who seems to manage his business properly, it is he, and if there is a well managed department, it is that of the Postmaster General, and the proof is to be found in the surplus which he obtains from year to year for the Minister of Finance, a surplus perceptible to the naked eye, and in regard to which he is worthy of congratulation. I also take this occasion of congratulating him on having remembered the small wage earners who never have many defenders, while the high officials always have many, besides being in a position to take care of themselves, which they do with courage and success.
There is a wide margin between a salary of $10,000 and another of $500. The distance which separates one from the other is great, I was tempted to say immorally so, in a democratic country such as ours. The man who earns $500 or $600 has a wife and children whom he cherishes just as does the man whose salary runs up to $10,000; his wife he must provide with clothing and nourishment ; his children he must clothe and feed and educate, exactly like the man who, one year with another, draws $8,000 or $10,000 of a salary. The former gets his $50 check per month, while the latter draws $700 or $800 per month ; the former will starve in the service of the people, while the other, if he leads an honest life, will not be able to spend his whole salary; one will be a pauper all his life, while the other will heap away money, grow rich, build up a fortune for himself at the expense of the public.
Mr. Speaker, the minister who will put an end to that state of things will go down to posterity as a benefactor of his country, and a grateful nation will dedicate a monument to his memory. The proper rule to follow in fixing the scale of salaries, is to grant to each man enough to live, bring up his family in accordance with the needs and requirements of the social environment in the midst of which he is called to live, and not the rule followed at present which ignores that elementary principle. Such a system is likely to cause large numbers to curse the fate which providence has assigned to them, and to build up on the

free soil of America an aristrocracy of the worst type, an aristocracy of wealth. Luxury side by side with misery in the service of the government and the people, is a thing which should not be tolerated. However, that state of thing exists, Mr. Speaker, and I have only to open the blue book to find numerous cases of men employed in the various departments, heads of families, who do not earn enough to ensure a comfortable living for themselves and family, while there are numbers of others who are unable to spend the whole of what they earn. I do not propose indulging in personal references in the course of the remarks which I have to make, nor attacking any one in particular. I shall refer to some high positions, but without in any way reflecting on those who were fortunate enough to secure such appointments. Moreover, my intention is not to hold the present administration wholly responsible for the evil, except in so far as they have made no attempt to cure it, but instead have allowed * it to grow worse, after promising implicitly, if not expressly, that they would apply a remedy, and though, in truth, they were in duty bound to do so.
For the time being and to start with, I shall be content with mentioning a few of these positions with large salaries attached. I may point out, in the first place, a few positions created by the present government; for instance, the Board of Commissioners appointed to supervise the building of the National Transcontinental Railway. At the outset, three commissioners were ap pointed; later on, a fourth commissioner was named. The chairman's salary is $8,000 per annum; the three others receive $7,000 per annum each. These salaries are too high, and moreover, there are too many commissioners. Would not two commissioners have been able to cope with the work?
Then we have the Railway Commission, an institution which I admire, and whose work will soon extend over the whole Dominion. At first they were three in number; a chairman and two commissioners. To-day there are six of them, and their salaries are as follows:	the president gets $10,000
per annum, the vice-president, $9,000, and the other commissioners $8,000 each.
The Civil Service Commission comprises two commissioners, each of whom draws a salary of $5,000 per annum.
The deputy ministers are to-day very numerous. They are growing in numbers day by day, and their salaries are increasing at the same rate. Once more, I am only stating the facts, and although I have worked the matter up carefully, I may have made some mistakes. If so, I shall be glad to be set right and corrected. In the Privy Council, in the Department of Militia, in that of Agriculture, in the Department of the Secretary of State, in the
Library, in the Public Works Department, in short, in all the departments, numbering fourteen in all, there are to be found deputy ministers, or head officers designated at times under some different names, but drawing the salary of a deputy minister, and these gentlemen, if I am not mistaken, number in all thirty-three. There salaries run from $4,500 to $8,000 per annum. There are two with salaries of $4,000, twenty two or twenty-four drawing about $5,000; five drawing $6,000, one $7,000, and lastly one drawing $8,000.
The ministers, who number fourteen, draw salaries amounting to $9,500, including their sessional indemnity, while the Prime Minister draws altogether $14,500. By the way, let me state that I am not objecting to the salaries granted to he ministers of the Crown; in fact I consider that their remuneration is inadequate, as compared with that of their deputy ministers. They have to undergo elections, and it is well known that, in regard to the Liberal party as well as to the Conservative, elections are an expensive thing and cannot be carried on solely by means of prayers. There devolve on the ministers social duties much more onerous than those devolving on the deputy ministers.
The judges of the Supreme Court of Canada are six in number, the Chief Justice, and five puisne judges. The Chief Justice gets a salary of $10,000 per annum, the five others, $9,000 per annum. There is also a judge of the Exchequer court who is paid $8,000 per annum. Then there are judges for the provincial courts whose salaries run from $3,000 to $8,000 per annum, besides their travelling expenses, which make up quite a large amount, reaching in several cases $1,100 and as high as $1,300 per annum. Six have received over $1,000 for travelling expenses. The expenditure in connection with these salaries and travelling expenses, reaches in the aggregate $1,075,536.81, for the year 1907-08.
In the Yukon we have three judges drawing $10,000 each per annum, in all $30,000. The administration of justice in the Yukon entails an expenditure of $88,088.47, and I understand the population is on the decline. According to the last census, that of 1901, it numbered only 27,219. The population of the country as a whole barely reaches 7,000,000, but for the purpose of my argument, I shall take it at that figure.
I have pointed out the high salaries which the Dominion government pays to its officers. Now, let us see how these things are managed in the United States. Our neighbours to the south of us are older and richer than we are. They number 87,971,000 in the United States proper ; while, with the islands taken in, the population

reaches 96,850,000. Taking the United States proper with all their denominations, )we have a total population of 105,000,000.
Now, let us see what salaries they pay. The figures which I am about to quote, are taken from volume 34 of the Senate documents, 59th Congress, 1906-07, appropriation for the year closing June 30, 1908. The United States have nine state departments called secretaryships or departments of state. They are as follows:	Agriculture, Treasury, War, Navigation, Postoffice, Interior, Commerce, Labour, and Justice, that is the department of the Attorney General. The various secretaries or ministers, heads of these departments, receive salaries of $12,000 each. Up to February 26, 1907, they were paid only $8,000. It was not until the year 1907-08, that they obtained that increase for the first time. The under-secretaries are paid on the average $4,500 per annum. There are several under-secretaries, whose salaries vary according to the importance of the various departments; but I repeat it, many of these under-secretaries get only $4,500 per annum. The chief clerks are paid only $2,500 or $3,000 at most.
In the Department of Agriculture, for instance, the under-secretary gets $5,000, but his department is somewhat more important than ours, since its appropriations for the year 1907-08 reach $9,444,290, equal to about one-eighth of our whole Supply Bill, and about eight times larger than the amount voted for our Department of Agriculture, which that same year amounted to $1,481,091.67, and for 1909, aggregates $1,112,500. Notwithstanding which our deputy minister of Agriculture draws a salary of $6,000 per annum.
The Postmaster General has a first assistant who draws $5,000 per annum. The secretary of the Department of Commerce and Labour has also an assistant and two under secretaries who draw $5,000 each. The assistant to the Attorney General draws $7,000, and the assistant to the Solicitor General, $7,500. One would be inclined to think that they have copied our scale of salaries or that we have copied theirs, seeing that we pay our deputy minister $7,000 and our solicitor $7,500.
While, as a rule, the salaries paid to their deputy ministers or under-secretaries are smaller than those we pay to our 33 deputy ministers in Ottawa, on the other hand, as regards subordinate officers, I find a smaller proportion of those starvation salaries to which I referred a moment ago, and on which no man can be expected to support a family.
Ambassadors and plenipotentiaries of the United States to England, Germany, Japan, Russia and other countries of the same standing, draw a yearly salary of $17,500. Extraordinary envoys and plenipotentiaries Mr. NANTEL.
to Belgium, China, Spain and other countries of the same class, draw $12,000.
The same officers representing the United States in Chili, Columbia, Peru, Roumania, Servia, Persia, and Siam brought $10,000 per annum. The envoy to Liberia, who fulfils the duties of consul general draws $5,000; the consul general to Cairo draws $6,000.
We have not as yet representatives of Canada in foreign countries; but we have in this very city of Ottawa, as members of the Railway Committee and of the National Transcontinental Railway board of commissioners, officers who draw salaries reaching seven, eight, nine and ten thousand dollars per annum.
At the congressional library, at Washington, the total salaries amount to $18,140. At the Dominion library of Ottawa, the salaries reach $25,685.50; and if the further increases are taken into account, the total amount will almost be double that of the salaries paid out for the same purpose by our neighbours.
The Civil Service commissioners at Washington receive only $4,000 per annum. Our commissioners here draw a salary of $5,000 each. The Washington War Department comprises what is known as the Office of Public Buildings and Grounds, apparently under the management of an assistant engineer, who draws $2,400 per annum and of a chief clerk whose salary is also $2,400 per annum.
Let us now come to the courts. The United States Supreme Court consists of a chief justice and eight puisnes judges. The chief justice is paid $13,000 per annum and the puisne judges $12,500 each. There are 29 circuit court judges, whose salary is $7,000 ; 70 district court judges, with a salary of $6,000 per annum. There are also six additional judges, appointed to meet the needs of the new territories. They also draw $6,000 per annum. The unorganized territories have eight judges with salaries of $5,000. The district or territory of Hawaii has three judges. The court of appeal for the district of Columbia consists of three judges, one of whom gets $7,500, and the two others, $7,000 per annum. The Supreme Court of that same district consists of six judges at $6,000 each. For all these judges, except those in Alaska, Arizona and Hawaii, appointed under federal authority, the total of salaries is $969,000, while for our Dominion judges, the total expenditure is $1,075,536.81, that is to say an over-expenditure in our case of $106,536.81.
The administration of the territory of Alaska, apparently entails on the people of the United States an expenditure of $67,000 per annum. The population is 32,000; the governor draws a salary of $3,000, and there are three judges with salaries of $5,000 each. The territory of Arizona has a

governor whose salary is $3,000; the territory of New Mexico a governor with a salary of $3,000. Our Yukon territory for judicial purposes only costs us $88,088.47 per annum. If we add to that figure the salaries of three other chief officers, we reach a total of over $104,000, that is $47,000 more than what the United States have to spend. The cost of management of the territory of Alaska as compared with that of the Yukon, shows how extravagant we are.
In the United States, barring the federal Supreme Court, I found no judges with a salary of $10,0000. The average runs from $5,000 to $6,000. On the other hand, in the territory of Arizona the judges get only $3,000. We have here many judges of superior jurisdiction who get only $3,000, while in the Yukon we have three judges drawing $10,0000 each, that is a total of $30,000, to administer the law to 27,219 people, provided their number has not gone down since the last census. These judges at $3,000 are not treated as well as subordinate officers at Ottawa, drawing the high salaries to which I have referred. Without some personal income these magistrates are unable to live up to the requirements of their position. They are starvelings, and I cannot conceive a worse situation than that of the man compelled to play the person of consequence on an empty purse.
I estimated the population of Canada as
7.000.	000. That of the United States proper reaches 87,971,000. If all their dominions are included, that figure should be raised to
105.000.	000. The cost of government here is $16.09 per head. In the United States, it amounts to $8.67, or $10.47 according that one or the other of the above figures is taken as representing the total population. Am I not justified in stating that our expenditure is extravagant?
I find another evidence of that extravagance in the pensions granted to some former officials. It is a matter which I have some hesitation in taking up, but I think it is my duty to do so. I am not attacking individuals, but merely a system. I refer to the judges. I consider that our system of pensions to superannuated judges rests on a false principle, on a principle of class legislation, which is always hateful and condemnable.
(Translation.) Does my hon. friend comprise in the list of superannuated judges the member for St. Anne's (Mr. Doherty)?

(Translation.) I except nobody. I am not criticising the hon. member for St. Anne's. I can only say that the hon. member has availed himself of the law, and it would not have been the part of so intelligent a man to omit doing so. In volume I of the Auditor General's report, page G-17, I notice the name of an ex-judge who draws a pension of $10,000, and I am satisfied that he has no children to bring up and send to school.
Please give us his name.
(Translation.) I do not like to mention any name. The hon. member will find out for himself by referring to page G-17, of the Report of the Auditor General, from which I am quoting.
(Translation.) Will the hon. member say whether it is not to the hon. Mr. Justice Routhier that he is referring?

(Translation.) No, it is to the Hon. Mr. Justice Taschereau, of the Supreme.'Court. You are putting me under the necessity of giving his name; you will be to blame for it. Another judge draws a pension of $8,000, and besides for the year 1907-8, he has drawn a further salary as judge of the Admiralty Court. Another pensioner draws $5,000. We pay altogether under this head $126,359.82. That also is ex- . travagance.
That legislation providing for the superannuation of judges, as enacted, is to say the least, overdrawn. It goes too far when it states, as will be found by referring to volume 3, chapter 138 of the Revised Statutes: " If any judge who has continued in the office of judge for fifteen years or upwards, or ('and' should have been put in here instead of, 'or') who becomes afflicted with some permanent infirmity, disabling him from the due execution of his office, resigns his office, &c." he is entitled to two-thirds of his salary for the remainder of his life. And please observe, even if he be only 45 or 50 years old. Section 20 states: if he has reached the age of 75 and has been a judge for 20 years; if he has reached the age of 70, and has been 25 years a judge, or if he has been 30 years a judge, whatever be his age, he is entitled to his full salary in each case at the time of his resignation, and that as long as he lies. While in office, that judge is not called upon to contribute a dollar to a pension fund. And see how solicitous the legislator appears to be: the benefit of that provision has been extended to the president of the Railway Commission, while the vice-president has been left out, although he may be in precisely the same position as the president. How admirable, Mr. Speaker, is that great solicitude shown on behalf of the president of that commission. Section 23 of the Act just quoted, provides that if the office of judge, which that nresident may have relinquished to accept the chairmanship of the commission, should later on entitle its occupant to a higher rate of salary, say $12,000 or $15,000, that same president would be en-

titled, even after being superannuated as president of the Railway Commission, to get that increase.
These high officials do not contribute one dollar to the superannuation fund out of which they will later on be paid as pensioners of the State, wihile subordinate clerks who get only $500 or $600 of a salary are called upon to contribute each month to that fund at the rate of 1, li, 3, or 3i per cent, according to their status and depending on the fact whether they draw $600 or more per annum, and whether they have joined the service previous or subsequently to a certain date. Then in order to be entitled to that pension, it is necessary that one should have been in the service of the State ten years or more, have reached the age of 60, and have become incapacitated through infirmity or otherwise. The pension is based on the average salary and it is a rather complicated affair to obtain it. It is granted by fractions of one-fiftieth per year of service. If the head of the department should make an unfavourable report, if the clerk should have been unfortunate enough to displease one of these gentlemen, his pension may be reduced. It is not even stated to what extent that reduction may be affected; that is left to the discretion of the deputy head or the minister. It is a rather difficult matter to get through the meshes of such an act. I believe it is Solon who said that laws are like a spider's web, which stops flies and other insects but through which birds easily pass. Solon lived 600 years before Christ but this truth still holds good to-day. Look into the act providing pensions for high officials, and you may be inclined to think that the legislator has purposely woven a web of such a fabric that high officials might easily get through, while others would be captured.
Why should there be two weights and two measures? I sincerely believe that we should change such a state of things, without, of course, interfering with vested rights. Therein lies a real evil, and the law should be amended so as to be more equitable and fair to all. Nowhere else is such a law to be found. I am not an iconoclast, but if we are intent on managing things economically, that law should be changed as soon as possible. Do not attempt economy at the expense of the small wage-earners while letting the higher officials go scot free.
It is geting late, Mr. Speaker, and while I might go on speaking of a good many other things,-since we are allowed in connection with the budget to refer to various matters,-I shall cut short my remarks for the time being.

(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, I crave the indulgence of the House for undertaking at this late hour of the night to answer briefly the remarks made by my hon. friend and neighbour the hon. member for Terrebonne.
I merely wish briefly to take exception to certain peculiar and eocentric statements uttered from his lips; for instance, his concluding remarks to the effect that any question whatsoever can be discussed on the budget. That is surely a new doctrine. I am at a loss to imagine where my hon. friend could have got acquainted with constitutional and executive law; but assuredly he cannot have followed the same curriculum that I have, for this is the first time I ever heard this theory expounded. 1 came to Ottawa with a strong settled purpose of talking little but listening much. I wished to learn something and I have just learned from my hon. friend, that anything can be spoken on the budget. It is evident that he and I are not agreed upon this subject.
My hon friend spoke of the pension law. As I did not wish to misquote him, I have endeavoured rather to get at the real meaning of his words and if I mistake not, I believe he is opposed to such a law as that. I do not entirely disagree with him on this point. Rut before attempting to improve or repeal a statute, it is well that one should look at what was done not very long since. I would understand the position taken by my hon. friend had he the courage of his convictions, and were he, before this session is over, to call for the repeal of that pension law which favours all those whom he termed the dregs of power. Such are the words he uttered.
(Translation.) I never used that word. I said budget-fed.

(Translation.) Well, let it be so, and I will help him if he likes to define what is properly meant by the budget-fed friends of the party, accentuating the expression if he so desires. It will be recalled that the legislation which was abrogated had been placed in our statute books in order to favour your ex-ministers, the late Sir A. P. Caron, Sir Mackenzie Bowell, and, last but not the least, the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster). Are the gentlemen intended by my hon. friend for Terrebonne (Mr. Nantel) to be the satiated of power? Or was the word aimed at such of his friends whom he called intelligent for benefiting by a statute passed quite a few years ago granting a pension to judges after fifteen years service? At all events, I would like to know what he thinks of those men who, as in the case of Yamaska county, went out campaigning against the government candidates, while at the same

time receiving a good big fat pension from the government, under pretense of physical disability, or of him who, not satisfied with getting such a substantial pension, got elected a member of this House to secure the $2,500 indemnity attached to the job. I hardly think the hon. member knew what he was talking about when expounding such a principle in the tone he assumed before the House a while ago. The hon. member also alluded to what took place when the Postmaster General asked the House to increase the salary of certain employees of his department. The government have already started increasing the salaries. They have appointed a Civil Service Commission, and increased the salaries of the inside service. If I mistake not it is their intention to pursue that wise policy. A little consistency does not hurt anyone, not even the hon. gentlemen opposite, who have been clamouring ever since the session started that the government are spending extravagantly. I will merely answer to them:
' Gentlemen, tune your fiddles.'
My hon. friend thinks that as a whole, this pension law is nothing but a perfect squandering of the public money, inasmuch as the beneficiaries of it never have contributed one dollar into the pension fund. He is mistaken. Let him look at the statute and he will see there that the government hold back upon their employees' salaries a certain sum which in their old age will be refunded to them. I hold the public servants in high respect, and I do not want to see them go a begging when old. As regards the increase of the smaller salaries, let him look at that particular branch of the service with which I - am especially acquainted, I mean the employees of the penitentiary. Their salary under the old regime was $500 only, but I was successful in having it raised to $600. This is again a happy reform brought on by the present government, which shows their good will towards the humbler offices of the service. Of course the hon. member, who was elected a Tory, dared not, and I know the reason why, attack the policy of his friends when they were in power.
He finds fault with the expenditure connected with the library, which he thinks, is out of proportion with those in the Washington library. I believe he was in Washington in his mind only. Had he been there at all, he would know how things are carried on there. I do not doubt of the correctness of the figures he quoted, but he does not know perhaps that the library at Washington cost $8,000,000 ; that electrical appliances and contrivances are in use which do away with perhaps one hundred employees. I invite him to call personally. Ours did not cost that amount, and I am not surprised at the number of employees which is required to give us an adequate
service. It is therefore practically impossible to cut down expenses in that direction.
Such were the few observations I had to offer on the question of the pension law.
I will conclude by referring to my hon. friend's first declaration. He was shocked at the Finance Minister capitalizing what was now lying at the bottom of the river near the city of Quebec. Had the Minister of Finance done what the hon. member for Terrebonne says he did, there is no question he could be held up to ridicule. But is that what he really did ? My hon. friend is a very clever finance man in St. Jerome ; he is even wealthy and I congratulate him. Let us take this for example: If he loaned $6,000 and the borrower did not pay him, would he charge this transaction to his revenue account or to capital account at the end of the year P He would beyond doubt, charge it up to capital account. That is precisely what the Finance Minister did in charging this operation to capital. It is thus also for all monies spent on the National Transcontinental. They all go to make up this country's assets. That is my way of understanding public finances. When I take out of my capital a certain sum of money, I cannot but help debit my capital with a like sum. The hon. Finance Minister seems to me to have figured out in the same manner.
(Translation.) Should you lose all your capital, would you still figure it out as your capital ?
(Translation.) If I lose all my capital, I charge the amount against my capital account, and the result is nil.
(Translation.) You will not come out of it as wealthy.

(Translation.) Of course not. Supposing my farm is worth $10,000, and I borrow $10,000 on it. Practically I do not own a farm any more, but will that keep me from deriving the revenue from that farm for the time being ? It seems to me a skilful financier like my hon. friend, would be able to understand such a clear argument.
With these few remarks, Mr. Speaker, I will now Tesume my seat. I would have several observations to make yet, but I want my hon. friend from Terrebonne to sleep upon his speech, and I hope his slumber will not be too much disturbed.

Mr. Speaker, as the hour is getting pretty late I will promise not to keep you very much longer. Since the budget speech was delivered we have heard a great many different kinds of arguments, but it strikes me that what the farmer and the average business man want to know is what amount of taxes they are paying at the present time.

By looking at the record we will find that in 1896 each man, woman and child in Canada was paying $5.48 in taxation while at the present time we find that we are paying $11 per head. While we find that the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) showed a surplus on the year's business we also find, by looking at the records, that we are $46,000,000 farther in debt. It struck me very forcibly how this would affect the province that I come from. By going into the figures I find that the province of Manitoba's share of this debt is something over $5,000,000. We have in that province about 9,000,000 acres of land under cultivation, and the debt of last year means a mortgage of $400 on every section of land under cultivation in the province of Manitoba. I would like to ask the Minister of Finance what the debt of this country will be at the end of four years. I had read a good deal about the Minister of Finance but I had never seen him until I came to this House. From what I had read and heard of the Minister of Finance I never knew of him as a joker until he delivered his budget speech. I am sure that the Minister of Finance must have been trying to get off a joke when he told the House that this government was a government that had held the land for the settler. I wonder if he forgets that almost the very first action of this government, after they came into power in 1896, was to try and give 375,000 acres of our western land to Mackenzie and Mann. Does he remember this government selling 250,000 acres of our homestead lands in the west for the paltry sum of $1 an acre? Every government that has ever held power in Canada, whether Reform or Conservative, has always held the homestead lands as a sacred trust of the people, but when this government came inlto power they sold even the homestead lands. They sold thousands and thousands of acres of our best coal lands to speculators and their friends. They gave leases of thousands and thousands of acres of our beat grazing lands for a paltry sum and in some cases people could get these leases for almost a song. Does the Minister of Finance forget this government selling hundreds of miles of fishing rights in the western country for $10 per year, or, does he forget the timber limit deals that were put through by this government or that they even went so far as to traffic in the Indian lands? They were not .satisfied with dealing in the white man's lands but we find that they took advantage of the Indians. The Indians are the same as orphans in this country; they are the wards of the people, we have charge of their resources and yet this government go to work and sell to their friends 39,000 acres of their land for $9,017. The purchasers, in a few weeks, in fact, before the Mr. W. H. SHARPE.
deed is made out to them, turn it over to speculators for $101,813, thereby cleaning up, out of the Indian lands, over $90,000. Mr. Speaker, we have heard a good deal during this session about a man they call Bill Miner. Bill Miner took his life in his own hands, you may say, when he went into the Rocky Mountains, held up the Canadian Pacific Railway express and stole a sum of money from it. I consider that Bill Miner is a prince beside these men who hide themselves behind the law and rob the orphans of the country. I do not intend occupying the time of the House very long, but there is a matter I wish to bring before the government and the House and that is in connection with an interview that the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Sifton) gave his newspaper in Winnipeg on the 10th February last. It is as follows:
Bluff and Bluster-Mr. Sifton's Comment on
Mr. Roblin's Defence of the Voters' Lists.
Hon. Clifford Sifton, who arrived in the city Monday from Ottawa, was interviewed yesterday in regard to Mr. Roblin's statement in the legislature regarding the provincial voters' lists. Mr. Roblin claimed that the lists were clean and satisfactory.
Mr. Sifton said that the statement of Mr. Roblin was untrue and that Mr. Roblin knew it to be untrue. The lists were flagrantly stuffed as every one knew perfectly well who had anything to do with the late election.
The assertion of the provincial premier, Mr. Sifton said, was a piece of impudent bluff and bluster.
When the last election was over the right hon. Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) asked the hon. member for Brandon the reason why the elections had gone against him in the province of Manitoba, and the hon. member for Brandon made practically the same reply to the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister repeated that same statement, or pretty nearly the same statement, on the 22nd January last in this House. I claim that if the statement made by the Prime Minister on the floor of this House on the 22nd January last is true, and if the the statement made by the hon. member foT Brandon in this interview with the Winnipeg ' Free Press ' is true, I, for one, have no right to a seat in this House. If those statements are false, as I claim they are absolutely false, then the hon. member for Brandon has no right to a seat in this House. I do not intend to discuss the merits and demerits of the Manitoba voters' lists at the present, time, more than to say that the electoral lists for the province of Manitoba are the fairest lists that are compiled in Canada to-day. The judges have complete charge of the lists in that province and there cannot be one name added or one name stricken off without the sanction of the judges. I was elected in the constituency of Lisgar, Manitoba, by 105 majority, and if this government will ap-

point a royal commission to inquire into the lists in that constituency, and if they can find 106 Conservatives improperly put on that list, or if they can find 106 Reformers improperly left off that list, I will resign my seat, provided, the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Sifton) will agree to resign his seat if his statements are not true, as I claim they are not true. I hope, Mr. Speaker, T make myself clear on this question. As the hour is very late I will resume my seat.
On motion of Mr. Nesbitt, the debate was adjourned.
